regions.name: Okanagan Valley
regions.tagline: A 200 km string of lakes from the Sonoran-edge desert at Osoyoos to the cool orchards of Lake Country.
regions.summary: The Okanagan Valley GI runs about 175 km north to south along a chain of glacial lakes (Okanagan, Skaha, Vaseux, Osoyoos). The south around Oliver and Osoyoos is the hottest, driest corner of Canada, where the Black Sage Bench and Golden Mile Bench grow Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah and Malbec; the north around Kelowna and Lake Country is cooler and suits Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and sparkling wine. Eleven sub-GIs subdivide it (Golden Mile Bench 2015; Okanagan Falls 2018; Naramata Bench and Skaha Bench 2019; Golden Mile Slopes; six more in 2022).
regions.history: Pandosy's 1859 mission vineyard, Calona (1932), the post-1988 vinifera replanting, and an explosion of estate wineries after 2000 (Mission Hill, Burrowing Owl, Quails' Gate, Osoyoos Larose, Painted Rock, Blue Mountain).
regions.terroir: Glacial benches of sand, gravel and silt, alluvial fans and some granite; large lakes moderate temperatures; rainfall below 250 mm near Osoyoos to about 400 mm in the north.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: From ripe Bordeaux blends and Syrah to taut Pinot Noir, Riesling and sparkling.

regions.name: Quebec
regions.tagline: Hybrids under winter blankets, and the birthplace of ice cider.
regions.summary: Quebec's wine industry is young, cold and fast-growing, concentrated south of Montreal in Montérégie and the Eastern Townships (Brome-Missisquoi around Dunham is the historic heart), with vineyards also near Quebec City and on Île d'Orléans. Winters reach minus 30 degrees Celsius, so growers rely on cold-hardy hybrids (Frontenac, Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix) or protect vinifera by hilling soil over the trunks and covering rows with geotextile fabric. The IGP Vin du Québec requires 100 percent Quebec grapes.
regions.history: Jacques Cartier found wild vines on Île d'Orléans in 1535 and called it Île de Bacchus; Samuel de Champlain's European vines died in 1608. The modern industry began in the early 1980s around Dunham: Christian Barthomeuf planted Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise in 1980, and L'Orpailleur was founded in 1982. Barthomeuf also created ice cider (cidre de glace) around 1989, now a Quebec speciality with its own IGP.
regions.terroir: Glacial and slate-derived soils in the Appalachian foothills; continental climate with hot summers, short seasons and severe winters.
regions.grapes: Frontenac (noir, gris, blanc), Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir under cover.
regions.styles: Crisp whites, rosé, light reds, icewine, ice cider.
regions.classification: IGP Vin du Québec; IGP Vin de glace du Québec; IGP Cidre de glace du Québec.

regions.name: Nova Scotia
regions.tagline: Tidal valleys on the Bay of Fundy, crisp whites and world-class sparkling wine.
regions.summary: Nova Scotia has a few hundred hectares of vines and around 20 to 30 wineries, mostly in the Annapolis and Gaspereau valleys near the Bay of Fundy, whose enormous tides moderate temperatures. The province's identity rests on two styles: Tidal Bay, a crisp, low-alcohol blended white appellation (first vintage 2012), and traditional-method sparkling wine, led by Benjamin Bridge. L'Acadie Blanc, a hybrid bred in Ontario, is the signature grape.
regions.history: Governor Isaac de Razilly wrote in 1634 that 'Bordeaux vines' were doing well at La Hève (LaHave); the Acadians grew grapes in the 17th century. Roger Dial founded Grand Pré Winery in 1979; Jost Vineyards (1983) at Malagash followed.
regions.terroir: Cool maritime climate, short season; soils of sandstone, shale and glacial till.
regions.grapes: L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Geisenheim 318, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Marechal Foch, Lucie Kuhlmann.
regions.styles: Tidal Bay white blends; traditional-method sparkling; fruit wines.

regions.name: Baja California
regions.tagline: Desert valleys behind Ensenada where Pacific fog, granite and Mediterranean grapes made Mexico's wine country.
regions.summary: Baja California produces most of Mexico's wine (about 70 percent by ICEX's estimate; some sources say up to 80 or 90 percent) from valleys strung along the inland side of the coastal hills north and south of Ensenada. Valle de Guadalupe is the heart, with about 150 wineries along the Ruta del Vino (Highway 3), plus restaurants that made it famous. San Antonio de las Minas, Valle de Santo Tomás, Valle de San Vicente, Ojos Negros, Valle de la Grulla and Tecate round out the region. Every August the Fiestas de la Vendimia celebrate harvest.
regions.history: Dominican missions (Santo Tomás 1791, Guadalupe del Norte 1834) planted the first vines. Bodegas de Santo Tomás was founded in 1888. Russian Molokans settled Valle de Guadalupe from 1905. L.A. Cetto (Tijuana 1928) and Casa Pedro Domecq (1972) industrialised the valley, then Monte Xanic (1987), Château Camou, Casa de Piedra (1997) and the graduates of Hugo D'Acosta's La Escuelita created a boutique movement.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean climate with cold Pacific influence; dry summers, little winter rain. Decomposed granite and sandy alluvial soils; salinity and falling aquifers are serious problems.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Carignan, Zinfandel, Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Ripe, often blended reds with saline freshness; crisp whites from cooler Ojos Negros and San Vicente; rosé.
regions.classification: No legal appellations yet; Baja producers began an IGP process in December 2025.

regions.name: Coahuila
regions.tagline: A spring-fed oasis in the Chihuahuan Desert where the oldest winery in the Americas still makes wine.
regions.summary: Coahuila's Parras valley, at about 1,500 m, owes its name ('grapevines') to the wild vines Spanish explorers found around its springs. Casa Madero, founded as the Hacienda de San Lorenzo in 1597, is the oldest winery in the Americas still operating. The state also has vineyards in the Sierra de Arteaga near Saltillo, at higher elevations, and at Cuatro Ciénegas, where Bodegas Ferriño has made wine since the 19th century. Coahuila producers are pursuing a protected geographical indication.

regions.terroir: High desert valley with springs and irrigation; hot days and cool nights; alluvial and limestone-derived soils.

regions.name: Querétaro
regions.tagline: Sparkling wine and fresh whites at 2,000 m, holder of Mexico's first wine IGP.
regions.summary: Querétaro's vineyards lie on the high plateau around Ezequiel Montes, Tequisquiapan, Colón and Cadereyta, at about 1,800 to 2,100 m. Altitude makes days warm and nights cold, but summer rain and hail during ripening keep alcohol low and acidity high, ideal for sparkling wine and fresh whites and rosés. Freixenet de México (Sala Vivé) and La Redonda built the region in the 1970s and 1980s, and it now has more than 40 wine projects and the busiest wine tourism in central Mexico. In 2025 IMPI granted Querétaro Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine.
regions.history: Grapes have appeared on Querétaro's coat of arms since 1655. Modern viticulture began in the 1960s and 1970s with brandy and sparkling-wine companies.
regions.terroir: High plateau with volcanic and calcareous soils; summer monsoon rain; frost and hail risk.

appellations.name: Napa Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel
appellations.summary:
The most famous wine address in the Americas, approved in 1981 as California's first AVA and the second in the country after Augusta, Missouri. The AVA covers almost all of Napa County apart from the area around Lake Berryessa, so it includes the valley floor, both mountain ranges and the side valleys, and it contains 17 smaller AVAs.

Napa's reputation rests on Cabernet Sauvignon. The style that made it famous is ripe and dense, with blackcurrant, plum, cocoa and sweet tannin, often lifted by new French oak. Thoughtful producers have moved toward earlier picking and less oak since the 2010s, but generosity of fruit is the house signature. A Napa Valley label alone usually means a blend of sites, while the sub-AVAs and named vineyards tell you where on the map the wine comes from.

The valley is also a lesson in land politics. The Agricultural Preserve of 1968 forbade subdivision of the valley floor into lots smaller than 20 acres (later 40), which is why the valley still looks like farmland rather than the Silicon Valley sprawl a few miles south. Land values are now among the highest for any vineyard outside Burgundy and Champagne, and a ton of Napa Cabernet costs several times the California average.
appellations.terroir: Mediterranean climate with a strong north-south temperature gradient: cool and foggy near San Pablo Bay, warm toward Calistoga. Soils mix volcanic material from the Sonoma Volcanics, uplifted marine sediments and gravelly alluvial fans. Mountain vineyards above the fog line give smaller berries and firmer tannin.
appellations.nerd_note: Napa Valley was the first AVA approved in California (1981). Wines from any of its 17 sub-AVAs must also show 'Napa Valley' on the label under California's conjunctive labeling law.
contains: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley

appellations.name: Calistoga
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Charbono, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Napa's northernmost and warmest valley-floor AVA, approved in late 2009 after a long fight over the use of the name by a brand that sourced grapes elsewhere. It sits at the head of the valley under Mount St. Helena, where the valley floor narrows and is ringed by the Mayacamas and Vaca ranges.

Days are hot, but cool air spills in at night through the Knights Valley gap from the Russian River side, so the daily temperature swing is among the largest in Napa. The wines are bold and dark: Cabernet Sauvignon with real tannic grip, plus Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Charbono from old vineyards that never got replanted to Cabernet. Chateau Montelena, whose 1973 Chardonnay won the white half of the 1976 Paris tasting, is the most famous estate; Araujo's former Eisele Vineyard, now Eisele Vineyard estate, is its cult Cabernet.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils derived from Mount St. Helena and the Sonoma Volcanics, plus alluvial fans; hot afternoons and cold nights.
appellations.nerd_note: The town's name is a slip of the tongue: founder Sam Brannan meant to promise 'the Saratoga of California' and is said to have blurted 'the Calistoga of Sarafornia'. In 2024 TTB adjusted Calistoga's boundary when it created the neighbouring Crystal Springs of Napa Valley AVA.

appellations.name: Diamond Mountain District
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary:
A steep, small mountain AVA (2001) on the Mayacamas slopes just southwest of Calistoga, rising from about 120 to 670 m. The soils are volcanic ash and weathered lava, light and fast-draining, and the vines sit above much of the valley's heat. Cabernet Sauvignon here is dense, mineral and tannic in youth, and it is among the longest-lived in Napa.

Diamond Creek defined the place. Al Brounstein planted it in 1968 and from 1972 bottled separate Cabernets from neighbouring blocks with different soils (Volcanic Hill, Red Rock Terrace, Gravelly Meadow), an early and very Burgundian statement that site matters in California. Schramsberg's caves are dug into the same mountainside.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic ash, tuff and red lava soils on steep, mostly northeast-facing slopes; cooler and less foggy than the valley floor.
appellations.nerd_note: Brounstein reportedly brought his first Bordeaux cuttings in by way of Mexico, and Diamond Creek's block-by-block bottlings were among the first vineyard-parcel Cabernets in the United States.

appellations.name: Spring Mountain District
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling
appellations.summary:
Mountain AVA (1993) on the Mayacamas slopes directly west of St. Helena, from about 120 m to almost 800 m. Steep, terraced vineyards on a mix of volcanic and sedimentary soils give Cabernet Sauvignon with firm tannin, bright acidity and a herbal, forest-floor note, and they hold some of Napa's most interesting whites: Stony Hill's taut, unoaked Chardonnay (first vintage 1952) and Smith-Madrone's dry Riesling.

The district has deep history (Tiburcio Parrott's Miravalle mansion of the 1880s later starred as the house in the TV soap Falcon Crest) and recent scars: the 2020 Glass Fire destroyed or damaged several estates here, including Newton and Cain.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic and uplifted marine sedimentary soils, steep slopes, fog-free afternoons and cool mountain nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Pride Mountain Vineyards straddles the Napa-Sonoma county line, so it keeps separate records for grapes grown on each side. Spring Mountain Vineyard's 1973 Chardonnay finished fourth among the whites at the 1976 Paris tasting.

appellations.name: St. Helena
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Zinfandel
appellations.summary:
Mid-valley AVA (1995) around the town of St. Helena, where the valley floor is narrowest and the heat of the north meets the last of the bay's influence. It is the historic heart of Napa: Charles Krug founded the valley's first commercial winery here in 1861, Beringer followed in 1876, and Heitz, Spottswoode, Duckhorn and Corison all sit within a few kilometres.

Cabernet Sauvignon from St. Helena tends to be plush and ripe, with the warmth of the upper valley, while the benchland vineyards on the west side (Spottswoode, Corison's Kronos) give more perfume and finesse. Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc also do well.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Mayacamas on the west, heavier clay and volcanic soils toward the Vaca side; warm days with modest fog.
appellations.nerd_note: Beringer made sacramental wine through Prohibition and claims to be Napa's oldest continuously operating winery; its 1884 Rhine House is a Victorian copy of the family home on the Rhine.

appellations.name: Rutherford
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Rutherford (1993) is classic Napa Cabernet country, a band across the valley floor between Oakville and St. Helena. Its fame rests on the Rutherford Bench, gravelly alluvial fans on the west side where Beaulieu and Inglenook built the reputation of California Cabernet before and after Prohibition. André Tchelistcheff, Beaulieu's winemaker from 1938, summed up the place in a line every Napa guide quotes: it takes Rutherford dust to grow great Cabernet.

The 'dust' is a texture as much as a taste: a fine, cocoa-powder tannin and a savoury, dusty, dried-herb note over ripe blackcurrant. Inglenook's 1941 Cabernet and Beaulieu's Georges de Latour Private Reserve (from the 1936 vintage) are touchstones of American wine history.
appellations.terroir: Deep, well-drained gravelly loam on the western bench; heavier, more volcanic soils toward the Silverado Trail. Moderately warm with morning fog.
appellations.nerd_note: Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who made his fortune in the Alaska fur trade, founded Inglenook around 1880. Francis Ford Coppola bought the estate in 1975 and, in 2011, bought back the Inglenook name and restored it.

appellations.name: Oakville
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Oakville (1993) is the richest square mile in American wine. The western bench below the Mayacamas holds To Kalon, the vineyard H.W. Crabb planted in the 1860s and named from the Greek for 'the highest beauty'; Robert Mondavi built his winery on it in 1966, the first major new winery in Napa since Prohibition. Opus One stands across Highway 29, Harlan Estate is on the western hills above, and Screaming Eagle, Dalla Valle and the old Heitz Martha's Vineyard are minutes away.

Oakville Cabernet combines the depth of Rutherford with a little more freshness and polish: cassis, violets, graphite and long, fine-grained tannin. Vineyards on the western alluvial fans give the most perfumed wines; the eastern side toward the Silverado Trail has heavier soils and more muscular reds.
appellations.terroir: Gravelly alluvial fans from the Mayacamas on the west; volcanic-derived soils from the Vaca Range on the east; moderately warm, with fog burning off by late morning.
appellations.nerd_note: To Kalon today is divided among several owners (Mondavi/Constellation, Beckstoffer, Opus One, the Detert and MacDonald families), and Constellation's trademark on the name has been the subject of lawsuits.

appellations.name: Yountville
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Named for George C. Yount, who planted the valley's first vines in the late 1830s, Yountville (1999) sits where the valley floor starts to feel the bay: cooler and windier than Oakville, with clay-rich and gravelly soils around a few low volcanic knolls. Cabernet here is firmer and more savoury, and Merlot does well.

Dominus Estate is the flagship: Christian Moueix of Pomerol leased and later bought the historic Napanook vineyard (once owned by Inglenook's John Daniel Jr.), made his first Dominus in 1983, and in 1997 built a winery by Herzog & de Meuron whose walls are wire cages filled with local basalt. Domaine Chandon, Moët & Chandon's California outpost (1973), is also here.
appellations.terroir: Mixed alluvial and clay soils with volcanic knolls; marine air from San Pablo Bay moderates afternoons.
appellations.nerd_note: Dominus's gabion walls let air and light filter through the stones, cooling the cellar without much air conditioning.

appellations.name: Stags Leap District
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Petit Verdot, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
A tiny AVA (1989) of about 1,200 ha below the rocky palisades of the Vaca Range on the Silverado Trail. The bare volcanic cliffs soak up and radiate heat, while afternoon wind from San Pablo Bay funnels through and cools the vines, a combination that gives Cabernet Sauvignon of ripe, silky texture over a firm core, the 'iron fist in a velvet glove' of local cliché.

This is where Warren Winiarski planted the S.L.V. vineyard in 1970, next to Nathan Fay's pioneering Cabernet. His 1973 S.L.V. Cabernet won the red flight at the Paris tasting of 1976. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars (S.L.V., FAY, Cask 23) has been wholly owned by Marchesi Antinori since 2023. Shafer's Hillside Select, Clos du Val (founded 1972) and Pine Ridge are also here.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic rock and gravelly loam fans at the foot of the palisades; heat reflected from bare rock, cooled by afternoon bay breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: The AVA name carries no apostrophe at all: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars and Stags' Leap Winery fought for years over the name, a settlement let each keep its own punctuation, and TTB sidestepped the issue.

appellations.name: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley
match: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
The southernmost valley-floor AVA (2004) apart from Carneros, between the city of Napa and Yountville. Cool, foggy mornings and a long, even season suit Chardonnay, Riesling and Merlot as well as a more restrained, savoury style of Cabernet Sauvignon.

Trefethen is the anchor. Its 1886 Eshcol winery, one of Napa's surviving 19th-century wooden 'ghost wineries', was badly damaged in the magnitude 6.0 South Napa earthquake of 2014 and rebuilt. Trefethen's 1976 Chardonnay was judged best Chardonnay at the 1979 Gault-Millau 'Wine Olympics' in Paris.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Mayacamas and Dry Creek, deep gravelly and clay loams; marine-cooled.
producers: Robert Biale (Black Chicken Zinfandel sourced nearby)
appellations.nerd_note: Oak Knoll is one of the few Napa sub-AVAs whose official name includes 'of Napa Valley', a compromise to avoid clashing with other Oak Knolls.

appellations.name: Mt. Veeder
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Mountain AVA (1990) in the southern Mayacamas, west of the city of Napa, with vineyards from about 150 to 750 m on steep, forested slopes. Unlike the volcanic north, much of Mt. Veeder is uplifted ancient seabed: shallow, acidic sandstone and shale soils that keep yields tiny. The wines are taut and powerful, Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec with firm acid and dusty tannin that need years in bottle.

Mayacamas Vineyards, built around an 1889 stone winery, is the reference. Its 1971 Cabernet was in the 1976 Paris red flight and tied for third place at the 30th-anniversary rematch in 2006. The Hess Collection pairs mountain Cabernet with a museum of contemporary art.
appellations.terroir: Shallow, sedimentary marine soils (sandstone, shale) with some volcanic intrusions; steep slopes, cooler marine-influenced climate.
appellations.nerd_note: Mayacamas's 1970s Cabernets were famously hard in youth; bottles from the Travers era (1968 to 2013) are now prized for how slowly they evolved.

appellations.name: Atlas Peak
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Sangiovese, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
High mountain AVA (1992) in the Vaca Range northeast of Napa city, with vineyards from about 230 to 800 m. The elevation keeps summer afternoons cooler than on the valley floor, nights are cold, and the red volcanic soils are thin and rocky. Cabernet Sauvignon is fresh, dark-fruited and firmly built.

Atlas Peak Vineyards was founded in the 1980s by a partnership that included Piero Antinori, who planted Sangiovese here before it was fashionable; Antinori's Antica estate continues the link. On 8 October 2017 the Atlas Fire started on these slopes and burned through vineyards and homes across the district.
appellations.terroir: Shallow volcanic soils, red and rocky, on a high plateau and slopes; above the fog with cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Atlas Peak was one of the early AVAs defined largely by elevation and is a source of Sangiovese that pre-dates the 1990s 'Cal-Ital' boom.

appellations.name: Howell Mountain
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Viognier
appellations.summary:
The first sub-AVA lying wholly inside Napa Valley, approved in late 1983 and effective in January 1984, and still one of the most distinctive. It is a high plateau in the Vaca Range above St. Helena, and the boundary follows the 1,400-foot (about 430 m) contour, roughly the top of the summer fog layer. Vines above the fog get longer sun and cooler nights, in thin red volcanic soils and white volcanic ash (tufa).

The result is mountain Cabernet at its most monumental: deep colour, blue and black fruit, iron and graphite, and tannin that can take a decade to unwind. Randy Dunn's Howell Mountain Cabernet set the style from 1979. The stone wineries of Ladera (built 1886 for Brun and Chaix) and La Jota recall a 19th-century reputation for Zinfandel.
appellations.terroir: Above 430 m: red volcanic soils and white tufa ash, low fertility, sunny days above the fog and cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Howell Mountain was one of the first AVAs anywhere defined by elevation; the 2024 Crystal Springs of Napa Valley AVA was drawn to stop exactly at Howell Mountain's 1,400-foot line.

appellations.name: Chiles Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
A small, high side valley (1999) tucked into the Vaca Range east of the main Napa Valley, at about 250 to 370 m. Cold air drains into it at night, so it is cooler than the valley floor, with a long season and a later harvest. Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel are firm and fresh.

The valley takes its name from Joseph Ballinger Chiles, an early overland pioneer who received the Catacula land grant in 1844. Volker Eisele, who farmed here organically from the 1970s, was one of the leaders who defended Napa's Agricultural Preserve.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial valley floor and surrounding slopes, cooler nights from cold-air pooling.
appellations.nerd_note: Brown Estate, known for Zinfandel, is widely cited as the first Black-owned estate winery in Napa Valley.

appellations.name: Coombsville
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Coombsville (2011) is a horseshoe of hills east of the city of Napa, often described as the eroded rim of an ancient volcanic caldera. Close to the bay, it is one of Napa's coolest Cabernet areas, with fog and afternoon wind; harvest comes later and the wines show fresh acidity, red and black fruit and less overt alcohol.

Growers such as Tom Farella planted here in the 1970s, but the area was a secret source for valley wineries until the AVA gave it its own name. Syrah, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also grow well.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic tuff and ash on the slopes, alluvial fans below; cool marine influence from San Pablo Bay.
appellations.nerd_note: The name honours Nathan Coombs, who laid out the town of Napa in 1847.

appellations.name: Wild Horse Valley
appellations.summary: A small, cool upland valley (1988) on the ridge east of Napa city that straddles the Napa-Solano county line, with most of it in Solano County. At around 300 to 600 m and open to wind from the bay, it is one of the coolest corners of the Napa Valley AVA, suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Plantings are tiny and the name rarely appears on labels.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils on a windy upland; cool, marine-influenced climate.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of the few Napa sub-AVAs that lies mostly outside Napa County.

appellations.name: Los Carneros
appellations.summary:
Los Carneros (1983) straddles the southern ends of Napa and Sonoma counties along San Pablo Bay, and it was one of the first AVAs drawn by climate rather than county lines. Its name means 'the rams', for the sheep that once grazed its low, rolling hills. Fog and a near-daily wind off the bay keep it cool, and the shallow, dense clay soils restrain vigour.

That made it the natural home for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, first planted seriously by Louis M. Martini and Beaulieu (with Tchelistcheff) in the 1930s and 1940s, and later by Saintsbury (1981). Champagne and Cava houses followed: Domaine Carneros (Taittinger), Gloria Ferrer (Freixenet) and Artesa (Codorníu). Hyde and Hudson are its most famous grower vineyards; Larry Hyde's partnership with Aubert de Villaine of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti produces HdV.
appellations.terroir: Shallow, heavy clay loams over hardpan; persistent wind and fog from San Pablo Bay; one of the coolest parts of the North Coast.
appellations.nerd_note: Carneros wines can be labeled with Napa Valley or Sonoma Valley as well as Los Carneros, depending on which side of the county line the grapes grew.

appellations.name: Crystal Springs of Napa Valley
appellations.summary:
Napa's newest sub-AVA (effective November 2024) covers about 4,000 acres of the western face of the Vaca Range between St. Helena and Calistoga. TTB describes it as an all-hillside region: every slope is between 15 and 40 percent, mostly facing west to southwest, and the boundary runs from the 400-foot contour (where the foothills meet the frost-prone valley floor) up to the 1,400-foot contour where Howell Mountain begins.

About 30 vineyards cover some 230 acres. Afternoon sun and warm air draining off the slopes make it a warm Cabernet Sauvignon site with less frost risk than the floor below. The name comes from Crystal Springs Road and the springs that gave the road its name.
appellations.terroir: All hillside, 120 to 430 m, volcanic soils on west and southwest slopes; less frost than the valley floor and less elevation cooling than Howell Mountain above.
appellations.nerd_note: Creating it also moved Calistoga's boundary, after a grower showed that one 17-acre vineyard on North Fork Crystal Springs Road would otherwise have been split between two AVAs.

appellations.name: North Coast
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot
appellations.summary: A vast umbrella AVA (1983) of about 3.3 million acres covering the wine country north of San Francisco: most of Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties plus parts of Solano and Marin. It contains dozens of smaller AVAs and is mostly used for blends that draw on several counties, much as 'Central Coast' is used farther south.
appellations.nerd_note: TTB modified the North Coast boundary when it created the Petaluma Gap AVA (2017) and again for Long Valley-Lake County (2023); the 2024 Comptche AVA was deliberately left outside it.

appellations.name: Sonoma Coast
appellations.summary:
A huge AVA (1987) of more than half a million acres that runs from the Mendocino line to San Pablo Bay and reaches well inland. It was drawn so broadly that it lumps cold coastal ridges with warm inland flats, and its creation is usually traced to Sonoma-Cutrer, whose vineyards needed a single AVA to qualify for 'estate bottled' labels. For decades the name promised more coolness than many wines delivered, which is why growers on the true coast pushed for Fort Ross-Seaview (2011) and West Sonoma Coast (2022).

At its best Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are lean, saline and intensely perfumed.

TTB drew Sonoma Coast in 1987 around a 'marine climate' line, but because it reached far inland to the edge of the Sonoma Valley and Russian River, it included warm sites as well as cold ones. That is why growers on the true coast pushed for Fort Ross-Seaview (2011) and West Sonoma Coast (2022). The best Sonoma Coast wines still come from ridgetops near the ocean and from the cool southern hills around Petaluma, where winds and fog keep sugars low and acidity high.
appellations.nerd_note: Sonoma Coast contains the Russian River Valley, Green Valley, Petaluma Gap, Fort Ross-Seaview and West Sonoma Coast AVAs.

appellations.name: West Sonoma Coast
appellations.summary:
Approved in 2022, West Sonoma Coast (about 141,800 acres) is the 'true' Sonoma Coast that growers had wanted since the 1990s: the band nearest the Pacific, from the Gualala River to the Petaluma Gap area, including the ridges around Annapolis, Fort Ross, Freestone and Occidental. TTB accepted that topography, geology and the marine climate set it apart from the inland parts of the old Sonoma Coast AVA.

Vineyards sit on steep ridges between redwood forest, often above the fog, in cold, windy conditions with long hang time. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are tense and aromatic, Syrah is peppery and lean.
appellations.terroir: Marine sediments of the Franciscan complex and sandstone; strong marine influence with fog in the hollows and sun on ridgetops.

appellations.name: Fort Ross-Seaview
appellations.summary:
A ridgetop AVA (2011) of about 27,500 acres just inland from the ruins of the Russian colony at Fort Ross. The vineyards mostly sit above about 280 m (920 feet), above the marine layer, so they get sun while the valleys below are blanketed in fog, and cold air drains away at night. Yields are low and berries small.

David Hirsch planted here in 1980, Walt and Joan Flowers in 1989, and Helen Turley and John Wetlaufer's Marcassin estate followed. The Pinot Noirs combine coastal brightness with surprising concentration.
appellations.terroir: Steep ridges of Franciscan sandstone and shale along the San Andreas fault zone; above the fog line with large diurnal swings.
appellations.nerd_note: The San Andreas fault runs right along the base of the ridges here, and Hirsch Vineyards straddles terrain on both tectonic plates.

appellations.name: Petaluma Gap
appellations.summary:
One of the only AVAs defined by wind. Petaluma Gap (approved December 2017, effective 2018) covers about 202,500 acres in southern Sonoma and northern Marin, where a break in the coastal hills between Bodega Bay and San Pablo Bay funnels cold ocean air inland every afternoon. The petition cited afternoon wind speeds well above those of the surrounding areas.

Wind makes grape skins thicker and slows ripening while keeping acidity high, so the 4,000-odd acres of vines give Pinot Noir with deep colour and firm structure, and peppery cool-climate Syrah.
appellations.nerd_note: Wind was the main distinguishing feature in the petition, which made Petaluma Gap a test case for TTB's idea of what counts as terroir.

appellations.name: Russian River Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
California's most celebrated cool-climate Pinot Noir appellation (1983, expanded in 2005 and 2011), about 171,000 acres around the lower Russian River from Healdsburg south to Sebastopol. Fog rolls up the river and through the Petaluma Gap most summer nights and mornings, so days start cold, warm by mid-afternoon and cool again by evening. That pattern gives ripe red-berry and cola Pinot Noir with bright acidity, and rich, citrusy Chardonnay.

The Burgundian pioneers were Joseph Swan (first vintage 1969), the Rochioli family (Pinot from the late 1960s), Williams Selyem (first vintage 1981), Dehlinger and Kistler. Westside Road, along the river south of Healdsburg, is the Pinot Noir 'Golden Mile'. Old-vine Zinfandel and sparkling wine also thrive.
appellations.terroir: Goldridge sandy loam (ancient marine sandstone), alluvial river terraces and some clay; fog-driven daily temperature swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Burt Williams and Ed Selyem started as weekend garagistes; their 1987 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir won the California State Fair's top prize and made the label a mailing-list sensation.
contains: Green Valley of Russian River Valley

appellations.name: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
match: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
appellations.summary:
A small, foggy AVA (1983) in the southwestern corner of the Russian River Valley around Forestville, Graton and Occidental, one of the coolest parts of the larger valley. The soil is almost all Goldridge sandy loam. It is classic ground for sparkling wine and taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Iron Horse, founded by Barry and Audrey Sterling in 1976, made sparkling wines that were poured at the Reagan-Gorbachev summits from 1985 and at many White House dinners since.
appellations.nerd_note: Until 2007 the AVA was called 'Sonoma County Green Valley'; TTB renamed it to avoid confusion with Solano County Green Valley.

appellations.name: Chalk Hill
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A warm corner of the Russian River Valley (1983) east of Windsor, in hills above the fog. The 'chalk' is a misnomer: the pale soils are volcanic ash from Mount St. Helena's eruptions, mixed with river sediments. It is warmer than the rest of the Russian River Valley and better suited to Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Bordeaux varieties than to Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Northern Sonoma
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: An umbrella AVA (1985) covering most of northern Sonoma County, including the Russian River, Dry Creek, Alexander and Knights valleys, Chalk Hill and Rockpile. It was petitioned by E. & J. Gallo, whose estate vineyards span several of those valleys, and it is used mainly by producers blending across them.

appellations.name: Dry Creek Valley
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Syrah, Grenache
appellations.summary:
A narrow valley (1983) running 25 km northwest of Healdsburg, now dammed at its head by Lake Sonoma. Italian immigrant families planted Zinfandel and field blends here in the late 19th century, and many of those head-trained, dry-farmed vines survive on the gravelly benches. Dry Creek Zinfandel is the archetype: brambly blackberry, black pepper and spice, ripe but rarely jammy.

The valley floor's deep alluvial loam suits Sauvignon Blanc; David Stare's Dry Creek Vineyard (1972) was the first new winery here after Prohibition and championed the grape. Rhône varieties and Cabernet are increasingly important.
appellations.terroir: Gravelly, iron-rich red benchland on both sides of a deep alluvial valley floor; warm days, with fog reaching the southern end.
appellations.nerd_note: Ridge labels its Lytton Springs Zinfandel blend as Dry Creek Valley; the old vines there were planted around 1900 and include Petite Sirah, Carignan and Mataro.

appellations.name: Alexander Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
The upper Russian River valley (1984, expanded 1990s to 2008) from Healdsburg north to Cloverdale, named for Cyrus Alexander, who settled here in the 1840s. It is one of Sonoma's warmest areas, with less fog than the lower river, and it is the county's Cabernet Sauvignon heartland: round, plush and approachable, with soft tannin and notes of black cherry and cocoa.

Hillside vineyards on the Mayacamas side give darker, firmer wines. Jordan (1972) and Silver Oak's Alexander Valley Cabernet made the style famous; Simi has made wine at Healdsburg since 1876.
appellations.terroir: Deep alluvial loams on the valley floor, gravelly benches and volcanic hillsides on the east.

appellations.name: Knights Valley
appellations.summary: A small, elevated valley (1983) between Alexander Valley and Calistoga, at the southeast corner of northern Sonoma. Volcanic soils from Mount St. Helena and warm, sunny days give Cabernet Sauvignon of structure and depth, and Sauvignon Blanc. Beringer owns a large share of the vineyards; Peter Michael Winery, founded by British electronics entrepreneur Sir Peter Michael in 1982, is the star estate.

appellations.name: Rockpile
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
appellations.summary: A rugged, remote AVA (2002) of ridges above the west arm of Lake Sonoma, limited to land above about 240 m (800 feet). Thin, rocky soils, wind and sun above the fog give concentrated, spicy Zinfandel and Petite Sirah with firm structure. The name comes from Rockpile Ranch, homesteaded in the 1850s by an ancestor of the Mauritson family.

appellations.name: Fountaingrove District
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
A hilly AVA (2015) of about 38,000 acres in the Mayacamas foothills northeast of Santa Rosa, with around 500 acres of vines. It is named for Fountaingrove, the utopian Brotherhood of the New Life founded by Thomas Lake Harris in 1875. Kanaye Nagasawa, a young Japanese samurai who came with Harris, ran its winery and became one of California's leading winemakers before Prohibition.

Volcanic soils and elevation suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah. The October 2017 Tubbs Fire swept through the district, destroying Fountaingrove's famous 1899 Round Barn and hundreds of homes.
appellations.nerd_note: Nagasawa (1852 to 1934) is often called California's 'Wine King'; land laws against Japanese ownership meant his estate was lost after his death.

appellations.name: Pine Mountain-Cloverdale Peak
appellations.summary: A small mountain AVA (2011) of about 4,570 acres around Pine Mountain, a 900 m peak on the western flank of the Mayacamas above Cloverdale, straddling the Sonoma-Mendocino line. Vineyards sit roughly from 490 to 900 m, above the Alexander Valley heat and fog, in thin, rocky volcanic and sedimentary soils. Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc are dark, firm and mineral.
appellations.nerd_note: The petitioners first asked for 'Pine Mountain-Mayacmas'; the name was changed after objections that it could be confused with Mayacamas Vineyards on Mt. Veeder.

appellations.name: Sonoma Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Merlot, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
appellations.summary:
The 'Valley of the Moon' (1982), running from Carneros north to Santa Rosa between the Mayacamas and Sonoma Mountain. This is where Sonoma wine began: Mission San Francisco Solano (1823), General Vallejo's vineyards, Haraszthy's Buena Vista (1857) and Gundlach Bundschu's Rhinefarm (1858). Jack London ranched at Glen Ellen.

The south is cooled by San Pablo Bay; the north around Kenwood is warm, and its hillsides grow powerful Cabernet and Zinfandel. Old vineyards such as Old Hill Ranch (planted in the 1880s) carry Zinfandel field blends; Hanzell (planted 1953) is a Chardonnay and Pinot Noir landmark.

appellations.name: Sonoma Mountain
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A mountain AVA (1985) on the western side of the Sonoma Valley, above Glen Ellen, including Jack London's Beauty Ranch. Vineyards above the fog get sun and a long season, and thin volcanic soils keep yields low. Cabernet Sauvignon is fine-grained and savoury; Patrick Campbell's Laurel Glen (from 1981) defined it.

appellations.name: Bennett Valley
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2003) in the hills southeast of Santa Rosa, cooled by marine air that flows through the Crane Canyon gap from the Petaluma side. That coolness suits Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir. Matanzas Creek (1977), known for Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc and its lavender fields, is the best-known winery.

appellations.name: Moon Mountain District Sonoma County
appellations.summary:
A steep mountain AVA (2013) of about 17,600 acres on the western face of the Mayacamas above the Sonoma Valley, with 40 commercial vineyards at the time of the petition. Volcanic rock and red soils on west-facing slopes give dense Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel.

Monte Rosso, planted in the 1880s by Emmanuel Goldstein and bought by Louis M. Martini in 1938, is its most famous vineyard, with Zinfandel and Cabernet vines more than a century old.
appellations.nerd_note: 'Sonoma County' is part of the official AVA name to keep it from being confused with other Moon Mountains.

appellations.name: Mendocino
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The main AVA (1984) for the southern and central valleys of Mendocino County, including Anderson, Ukiah, Redwood and Potter valleys and McDowell Valley. It is used for blends from across those valleys; inland it means warm-climate Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan and Cabernet.

appellations.name: Anderson Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary:
A narrow, 25 km valley (1983) along the Navarro River that opens toward the Pacific, so fog and cool air pour in every evening. It is one of California's coolest wine valleys and its most Alsatian: Gewürztraminer, Riesling and Pinot Gris grow beside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and the valley hosts an annual Alsace festival.

Roederer Estate arrived from Champagne in 1982 and showed that the valley could make world-class sparkling wine; its L'Ermitage is a benchmark. Pinot Noir from the 'deep end' near Philo and Navarro is tense, floral and savoury.
appellations.terroir: Marine sedimentary soils on benches and slopes; fog and large daily temperature swings.
appellations.nerd_note: The valley had its own jargon, Boontling, invented by Boonville residents around 1900; a 'horn of Bahl' is a glass of good wine.

appellations.name: Mendocino Ridge
appellations.summary:
The only non-contiguous AVA in the United States (1997): it consists of every piece of land above 1,200 feet (366 m) in a coastal strip of southwestern Mendocino County, so its map looks like an archipelago of 'islands in the sky' poking above the marine layer. Old Zinfandel vineyards such as Zeni and Ciapusci, planted by Italian families, grow on these ridges alongside newer Pinot Noir.

In January 2024 TTB proposed renaming it 'Mendocino Coast Ridge' to stress its coastal identity; as of late 2026 that proposal had not been finalised.
appellations.nerd_note: Because only land above 1,200 feet counts, the AVA covers about 87,000 acres on paper but has only a few hundred acres of vines.

appellations.name: Yorkville Highlands
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
appellations.summary: Rolling, rocky hills (1998) along Highway 128 between Cloverdale and the Anderson Valley, at about 300 to 760 m. Gravelly, low-fertility soils and a climate between the warm Alexander Valley and the cool Anderson Valley suit Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Bordeaux and Rhône reds.

appellations.name: Redwood Valley
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Carignan, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A warm valley (1997) north of Ukiah, at the head of the Russian River watershed, with red, iron-rich soils. Italian families planted Zinfandel, Carignan and Petite Sirah here early in the 20th century, and Fetzer was founded here in 1968. Old vines still give some of Mendocino's best Zinfandel and Carignan.

appellations.name: Potter Valley
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A high, cool valley (1983) northeast of Ukiah, ringed by mountains and fed by water diverted from the Eel River into the Russian River. Cold nights and a long season favour aromatic whites (Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc) and botrytised dessert wines, as well as Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: McDowell Valley
appellations.summary: A tiny bench valley (1982) east of Hopland at around 300 m. It is best known for old Syrah and Grenache, among California's oldest Rhône plantings (some vines date from 1919), which McDowell Valley Vineyards bottled in the early days of the Rhône Rangers movement.

appellations.name: Cole Ranch
appellations.summary: Once the smallest AVA in the United States (1983) at about 150 to 190 acres, a single ranch in a narrow valley in the hills between Ukiah and Boonville, owned by the Cole family. It grows Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Hawaii's Ulupalakua (2021) has since taken the 'smallest AVA' title.
appellations.nerd_note: Cole Ranch is essentially a one-owner AVA, which is legal as long as the petition proves the area is geographically distinct.

appellations.name: Covelo
appellations.summary: A remote, high valley (2006) of about 38,000 acres in northeastern Mendocino County, at about 425 m, surrounded by mountains and the Round Valley Indian Reservation. Cold winters and warm summers; plantings are very small.

appellations.name: Dos Rios
appellations.summary: A tiny, remote AVA (2005) of about 15,500 acres where the Middle Fork and main stem of the Eel River meet ('two rivers'), in rugged northern Mendocino County. It has only a few acres of vines.

appellations.name: Eagle Peak Mendocino County
appellations.summary: A mountainous AVA (2014) of about 26,260 acres northwest of Redwood Valley, with about 120 acres in 16 vineyards at the time of approval. The petition cited a marine-influenced climate, strong breezes, steep slopes and shallow soils with little water-holding capacity, which keep yields low for Pinot Noir and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Comptche
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2024) of about 1,422 acres around the hamlet of Comptche, a few kilometres inland from Mendocino town. Unusually, TTB excluded it from the North Coast AVA because its foggy, cold, coastal climate and soils differ so sharply from the larger area. It grows Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling-wine grapes on a handful of small vineyards.
appellations.nerd_note: Comptche is one of very few AVAs that is surrounded by, but not part of, a larger AVA.

appellations.name: Clear Lake
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Zinfandel, Merlot
appellations.summary: The large umbrella AVA (1984) around Clear Lake, covering most of Lake County's vineyards. The lake moderates temperatures, while altitudes of 400 m and more give cool nights. Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Sauvignon lead, with Petite Sirah and Zinfandel from older plantings.

appellations.name: Red Hills Lake County
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Petite Sirah
appellations.summary: Volcanic hills (2004, expanded 2024) on the flanks of Mount Konocti south of Clear Lake, at about 430 to 900 m. The red soils are full of obsidian and the light is intense, so Cabernet Sauvignon develops thick skins, dark colour and firm tannin, often with surprising freshness. Andy Beckstoffer's Amber Knolls and Obsidian Ridge are among its best-known vineyards.
appellations.nerd_note: The 2004 petition reported about 3,100 acres of vineyards; obsidian chips glitter in the soil after rain.

appellations.name: Big Valley District-Lake County
appellations.summary: A flat basin (2013) on the southwest shore of Clear Lake around Kelseyville, with about 1,800 acres of vines at approval. High water tables and cold-air pooling give a cooler, frostier site than the surrounding hills; Sauvignon Blanc is the signature.

appellations.name: Kelsey Bench-Lake County
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: A gently sloping bench (2013) between Big Valley and the Red Hills, at about 410 to 610 m, with about 900 acres of vines at approval. Better air drainage than Big Valley and deep, well-drained alluvial soils suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Sauvignon Blanc.

appellations.name: High Valley
appellations.summary: A narrow, east-west valley (2005) in northeastern Lake County above Clear Lake, at about 500 to 920 m. Cool air drains down from the surrounding ridges, giving a long season for Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet and Syrah. Its boundary was trimmed in 2023 when the neighbouring Long Valley-Lake County AVA was created.

appellations.name: Upper Lake Valley
appellations.summary: A valley (2022) at the north end of Clear Lake around the town of Upper Lake, about 17,360 acres. The petition stressed hydrogeology: a shallow water table fed by streams from the Mendocino National Forest, plus soils and a climate that differ from the rest of Clear Lake. Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Sauvignon dominate.

appellations.name: Long Valley-Lake County
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Petite Sirah
appellations.summary: A small, high valley (2023) of about 7,605 acres in northeastern Lake County, northeast of Clear Lake, with five vineyards (about 149 acres) and three wineries at approval. Elevation and cold winters distinguish it from High Valley, part of which it took over. Unusually, it lies outside the Clear Lake AVA; TTB adjusted the North Coast boundary to include it.

appellations.name: Guenoc Valley
appellations.grapes: Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: An early single-proprietor AVA (1981) in southern Lake County, on the old Guenoc Ranch. The English actress Lillie Langtry, a friend of the future Edward VII, bought the ranch in 1888 and hired a Bordeaux winemaker; her portrait was later used on the labels of Langtry Estate. Warm and dry, it grows Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc.

appellations.name: Benmore Valley
appellations.summary: A small, high valley (1991) in the Mayacamas on the western edge of Lake County, at about 730 m. Once planted mainly to Chardonnay for large brands, it now has few vines.

appellations.name: Solano County Green Valley
appellations.summary: A small valley (1983) in the hills of western Solano County, next door to Napa's Wild Horse Valley and east of Coombsville, cooled by air from San Pablo Bay through the Carquinez Strait. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay grow on gentle slopes. It was renamed in its current form to distinguish it from Sonoma's Green Valley.

appellations.name: Suisun Valley
appellations.grapes: Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A valley (1982) just east of Napa across the Vaca Range near Fairfield, among the first AVAs approved in California. Afternoon winds from the Suisun Bay cool it, and it grows Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel. Wooden Valley and Ledgewood Creek are among its wineries.

appellations.name: Capay Valley
appellations.summary: A long valley (2002) in western Yolo County along Cache Creek, between the Blue Ridge and the Capay Hills. Warm and dry, it grows Rhône and Mediterranean varieties on a small scale, and the area is known more widely for organic farms.

appellations.name: Dunnigan Hills
appellations.summary: Rolling hills (1993) in northern Yolo County beside Interstate 5, created at the request of R.H. Phillips, which planted large vineyards here in the 1980s. Warm days and Delta breezes; Syrah, Viognier and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Winters Highlands
appellations.summary: A small upland AVA (2023) of about 7,300 acres in the foothills west of Winters, straddling Yolo and Solano counties near the Napa line. The petition cited higher humidity and less rainfall than surrounding areas, plus distinctive soils; vineyards grow Bordeaux and Mediterranean varieties.

appellations.name: Clarksburg
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Petite Sirah, Chardonnay, Albariño
appellations.summary: Delta country (1984, expanded 2022) south of Sacramento, where vineyards grow on reclaimed river islands behind levees. Cool afternoon breezes through the Carquinez Strait make it cooler than Lodi. Chenin Blanc is the historic speciality, plus Petite Sirah and Albariño; much fruit is sold to wineries elsewhere.

appellations.name: Merritt Island
appellations.summary: A Delta island (1983) of about 5,000 acres inside Clarksburg, bounded by the Sacramento River and Elk Slough. Sandy loam over peat and cool Delta breezes; the Bogle family petitioned for it.

appellations.name: Willow Creek
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1983) along the Trinity River in eastern Humboldt and western Trinity counties, where coastal fog meets inland heat. A handful of growers make Zinfandel and Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Trinity Lakes
appellations.summary: A remote mountain AVA (2005) of about 96,000 acres around Lewiston and Trinity Lake in Trinity County, high in the Klamath Mountains. Vines are few and the climate is cool and continental.

appellations.name: Seiad Valley
appellations.summary: One of California's northernmost AVAs (1994), a tiny valley on the Klamath River in Siskiyou County near the Oregon border. It was established for a single grower and has almost no commercial vineyards today.

appellations.name: Inwood Valley
appellations.summary: A small valley (2012) of about 28,400 acres in eastern Shasta County, in the foothills of the southern Cascades east of Redding. At approval it had about 60 acres of vines; volcanic soils and cool nights from the Cascades suit Bordeaux and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Manton Valley
appellations.summary: A small valley (2014) of about 11,200 acres on the western slope of Mount Lassen in Shasta and Tehama counties. Volcanic soils from Lassen and elevations around 600 m give cool nights; a few small wineries.

appellations.name: Central Coast
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: Umbrella AVA (1985, adjusted 1999, 2006 and 2024) of about 6.8 million acres covering the coastal counties from Contra Costa and Alameda south to Santa Barbara. It is used for multi-county blends and contains famous AVAs from the Santa Cruz Mountains to Sta. Rita Hills.

appellations.name: San Francisco Bay
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah
appellations.summary: An umbrella AVA (1999) covering the counties around San Francisco Bay, roughly 2,450 square miles at creation, expanded in 2006, 2008 and 2024 (to take in all of the new Contra Costa AVA). It contains Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley, Lamorinda, Contra Costa and others and is used for blends from around the Bay.

appellations.name: Livermore Valley
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah
appellations.summary:
One of California's oldest wine districts (AVA 1982, expanded 2006), an east-west valley in Alameda County where cool air from San Francisco Bay flows in each afternoon. Gravelly soils reminded early growers of Graves; Charles Wetmore planted Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from Château d'Yquem cuttings in the 1880s, and his Cresta Blanca white won a gold medal at the 1889 Paris Exposition.

Carl Wente (1883) and James Concannon (1883) founded wineries that are still family-run. The Wente clone of Chardonnay, propagated from cuttings Ernest Wente obtained in 1912, is the ancestor of most Chardonnay planted in California. Concannon's Petite Sirah was the first varietal bottling of that grape (1961).
appellations.nerd_note: Most Chardonnay in California descends from the 'Wente clone', making Livermore the grandmother of the state's most planted white.

appellations.name: Santa Clara Valley
appellations.summary: The historic valley (1989) south of San Francisco Bay, now Silicon Valley. In the 19th century it had dozens of wineries, including Paul Masson's and Almaden (founded 1852 by Charles Lefranc), but urban growth erased most vineyards. Vines remain in the south around Gilroy, Morgan Hill and the Hecker Pass.

appellations.name: San Ysidro District
appellations.summary: A small district (1990) on the eastern side of the Santa Clara Valley near Gilroy, cooled by marine air through the Pajaro Gap. It mostly supplies Chardonnay and Pinot Noir to wineries elsewhere.

appellations.name: Pacheco Pass
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1984) at the pass through the Diablo Range between Santa Clara and San Benito counties. Strong marine winds; a few vineyards on the historic route to the San Joaquin Valley.

appellations.name: Lamorinda
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A small, hilly AVA (2016) in western Contra Costa County named for the towns of Lafayette, Moraga and Orinda. Many tiny vineyards (46 covering 139 acres at approval) on the slopes of the Berkeley Hills grow Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, cooled by bay fog.

appellations.name: Contra Costa
appellations.summary:
A new AVA (2024) of about 167,100 acres in eastern Contra Costa County, around Oakley, Brentwood and Antioch, with at least 60 vineyards on about 1,700 acres. Its treasure is ungrafted, century-old Zinfandel, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Carignan and Petite Sirah on deep, sandy soils where phylloxera never took hold, much of it bought by producers such as Bedrock, Cline, Turley and Ridge.

Creating it required TTB to enlarge both San Francisco Bay and Central Coast so that Contra Costa sits fully inside them.
appellations.nerd_note: The Evangelho Vineyard in Antioch, planted in the 1890s, grows own-rooted vines in deep sand dunes left by an ancient river delta.

appellations.name: Santa Cruz Mountains
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Merlot, Zinfandel
appellations.summary:
One of the first AVAs defined by its mountains (1982): the boundary follows elevation lines on both sides of the range, roughly above 400 feet on the ocean side and 800 feet on the bay side, to take in the slopes rather than the valleys. The range between Silicon Valley and the Pacific has vineyards scattered through redwood and oak forest, many above the fog.

Its history is outsized. Paul Masson made sparkling wine at Saratoga from the 1890s; Martin Ray founded Mount Eden in the 1940s and preached 100 percent varietal wines; Ridge's Monte Bello Cabernet (made under Paul Draper from 1969) placed fifth in the red flight at the 1976 Paris tasting and won the 30th-anniversary rematch outright in 2006. Rhys, Mount Eden and others make thrilling Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: Steep slopes of fractured Franciscan shale, sandstone and some limestone (Monte Bello); marine influence, fog in the valleys, and the San Andreas fault running through the range.
appellations.nerd_note: Ridge has printed full ingredient lists on its labels since 2011, a direct challenge to secretive winemaking.

appellations.name: Ben Lomond Mountain
appellations.summary: A small mountain AVA (1987) inside the Santa Cruz Mountains, on a ridge northwest of Santa Cruz above the fog line, at 120 to 800 m. Sandy soils from granite and limestone; cool Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Cabernet.

appellations.name: Monterey
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Large AVA (1984) covering the Salinas Valley and its side valleys. Cold wind blows up the valley from Monterey Bay every afternoon, so the north is among the coolest places in California and yields are high on the flat valley floor; the south around King City is warmer. Monterey is a major source of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling for big brands, with a small number of exceptional sites on the benches.

appellations.name: Santa Lucia Highlands
appellations.summary:
Terraced benches (1992) on the eastern flank of the Santa Lucia Range, facing east across the Salinas Valley, from about 30 to 370 m. Morning fog and fierce afternoon winds from Monterey Bay give a long, cool season, while the southeast-facing slopes catch the morning sun. The result is dense, dark-fruited, deeply coloured Pinot Noir and rich Chardonnay and Syrah.

The Pisoni family (Gary Pisoni planted from 1982) and Garys' Vineyard (with Gary Franscioni), Rosella's and Sleepy Hollow are the famous names.
appellations.terroir: Gravelly, well-drained alluvial terraces of granitic origin; strong afternoon winds.

appellations.name: Arroyo Seco
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: An AVA (1983, boundaries adjusted 2006, 2018 and 2021) around the Arroyo Seco river where it emerges from the Santa Lucia Range near Greenfield. The cool eastern section is known for Riesling and Chardonnay grown on 'Greenfield potatoes', rounded river cobbles that store heat. The warmer canyon to the west grows Cabernet and Zinfandel.

appellations.name: Chalone
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Chenin Blanc, Pinot Blanc
appellations.summary: A remote, high bench (1982) at about 500 m in the Gavilan (Gabilan) Mountains, under the volcanic spires of Pinnacles National Park. Its limestone and granite soils are rare in California, and vines were first planted here around 1919. Dick Graff bought the property in 1965 and made Chalone's Burgundian Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; its 1974 Chardonnay was third among the whites in Paris in 1976.
appellations.nerd_note: Chalone's water had to be trucked up the mountain for years; the Chenin Blanc vines planted in 1919 are among the oldest in California.

appellations.name: Carmel Valley
appellations.summary: A narrow valley (1983) running inland from Carmel-by-the-Sea, sheltered from fog at its upper end by the Santa Lucia Range, where vineyards sit at 200 to 600 m. It is warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; Durney Vineyards (later Heller Estate) planted the first commercial vineyard in 1968.

appellations.name: San Bernabe
appellations.summary: An AVA (2004) defined by one enormous vineyard south of King City in the Salinas Valley, at one time described as the largest contiguous vineyard in the world (more than 5,000 acres, owned by Delicato). Sandy, wind-deposited soils grow a range of varieties for large brands.

appellations.name: San Lucas
appellations.summary: A warm AVA (1987) in the southern Salinas Valley around San Lucas, beyond the reach of most of Monterey Bay's cold afternoon wind. Large vineyards on alluvial benches, some owned by Delicato, which petitioned for it, supply Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay to big producers.

appellations.name: Hames Valley
appellations.summary: The southernmost Monterey AVA (1994), a warm inland valley near the San Luis Obispo County line with wide day-night temperature swings. Shallow, rocky soils grow Bordeaux and Rhône varieties, mostly sold to wineries elsewhere in the Central Coast.

appellations.name: San Antonio Valley
appellations.summary: A remote valley (2006) west of the Salinas Valley in southern Monterey County, near Mission San Antonio de Padua (1771) and the Fort Hunter Liggett army base. Warm days and cold nights; Rhône and Bordeaux varieties and Zinfandel.

appellations.name: Gabilan Mountains
appellations.summary: A large mountain AVA (2022) of about 98,000 acres along the Gabilan (Gavilan) Range between the Salinas Valley and San Benito County, defined by elevation, a cooler climate and granitic and limestone soils. It encloses Chalone and Mt. Harlan, but TTB kept those older AVAs as they are.

appellations.name: San Benito
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Umbrella AVA (1987) for the winegrowing valleys of San Benito County, east of Monterey across the Gabilan Range, including Cienega Valley, Paicines and Lime Kiln Valley. Almaden once farmed thousands of acres here.

appellations.name: Mt. Harlan
appellations.summary:
A one-producer mountain AVA (1990) high in the Gabilan Range, about 670 to 790 m, created for Josh Jensen's Calera. After studying in Burgundy, Jensen searched California for limestone and found it on an old lime kiln site here; he planted Pinot Noir from 1975 in named parcels (Selleck, Reed, Jensen, Mills, de Villiers, Ryan).

The Pinots are lean, mineral and long-lived, and Calera's Viognier was one of the first in America.

Jensen planted his first three Pinot Noir parcels in 1975 at about 670 m, far from any town and with scarce water. Yields are very low because of the thin soils and drought. Calera's Pinots are known for long ageing: they start firm and savoury and open into mushroom, rose and red-fruit perfume after a decade. Jensen sold the winery to Duckhorn in 2017, and the estate continues to bottle each named parcel separately.
appellations.nerd_note: Calera means lime kiln in Spanish; the old kiln Jensen found on the mountain told him the limestone he wanted was there.

appellations.name: Cienega Valley
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Pfeffer, Négrette
appellations.summary: Historic valley (1982) in San Benito County along the San Andreas fault, where vines were planted in the 1850s. William Palmtag and later Almaden made wine here; DeRose Vineyards farms old, own-rooted Zinfandel and Négrette. Limestone and granite soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The vineyard sits directly on the San Andreas fault; the creep of the fault slowly bends rows and has cracked the old winery walls.

appellations.name: Lime Kiln Valley
appellations.summary: A tiny valley (1982) within Cienega Valley, named for lime kilns that once burned local limestone. Old vineyards grow Zinfandel and Mourvèdre on limestone-rich soils.

appellations.name: Paicines
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1982) in San Benito County south of Hollister, petitioned by Almaden, which once planted large vineyards here. Cool breezes; mostly grape-growing for other wineries.

appellations.name: San Luis Obispo Coast
appellations.summary: A coastal AVA (2022) of about 408,500 acres stretching the length of San Luis Obispo County west of the Santa Lucia Range, from the Monterey line to the Santa Maria River. It is cooled directly by the Pacific and encloses the Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley AVAs. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah are the focus.

appellations.name: Edna Valley
appellations.summary:
A cool, east-west valley (1982) just south of San Luis Obispo city, open to the Pacific through Morro Bay so that fog and wind flow straight in. It has one of the longest growing seasons in California, ideal for Chardonnay with crisp acidity and Pinot Noir. Soils include volcanic plugs (the Nine Sisters) and marine sediments.

Paragon Vineyard, planted by the Niven family from 1973, was the valley's pioneer and still supplies many wineries; the Nivens later founded Baileyana and Tangent, and Edna Valley Vineyard was a joint venture with Chalone. Because the valley points straight at the Pacific through Morro Bay, the afternoon breeze arrives early and the growing season can stretch from February budbreak to November harvest, giving Chardonnay its hallmark combination of ripeness and acidity. Since 2022 Edna Valley has sat inside the San Luis Obispo Coast AVA.
appellations.nerd_note: John Alban planted Viognier, Roussanne and Grenache here around 1990; Alban Vineyards bills itself as the first American winery founded exclusively for Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Arroyo Grande Valley
appellations.summary: A valley (1990) southeast of Edna Valley that grades from cool and foggy near the coast to warmer at its inland end. Talley Vineyards' Rincon and Rosemary's vineyards give fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; at the warmer top end, Saucelito Canyon farms Zinfandel planted in 1880.

appellations.name: York Mountain
appellations.summary: A tiny, cool AVA (1983) in the Santa Lucia Range between Paso Robles and the coast, at about 450 m. Andrew York founded a winery here in 1882, one of the oldest in the county; marine air makes it far cooler than Paso Robles, which is why TTB kept it separate.
appellations.nerd_note: York Mountain sits outside the Paso Robles AVA even though it is almost surrounded by it.

appellations.name: Paso Robles
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Petite Sirah, Merlot
appellations.summary:
The large Paso Robles AVA (1983, expanded 2009) covers about 610,000 acres and more than 40,000 acres of vines in northern San Luis Obispo County. Hot days, very cold nights and limestone-rich hills on the west side give powerful Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Rhône blends. Since 2014 it has been divided into 11 district AVAs.

The 2014 division into 11 districts came after a decade of debate and studies by the Paso Robles AVA Committee showing large differences in rainfall (from under 250 mm in the east to over 760 mm in the west), soils and temperature. Paso is also one of California's most ambitious Rhône regions: the Rhône Rangers movement of the 1980s and 1990s found its home here, and Saxum's James Berry Vineyard bottlings have been among the most highly scored American Rhône blends. Water is the key political issue, since the Paso Robles groundwater basin is overdrawn and the county has limited new plantings.

appellations.name: Adelaida District
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Roussanne, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: The northwestern hills of Paso Robles (2014), at 275 to 670 m in the Santa Lucia foothills, with calcareous shale and limestone soils, more rain than the east and cool nights. It is home to Tablas Creek, where the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel and importer Robert Haas planted French Rhône clones from 1989, and to Justin's Isosceles and Halter Ranch.

appellations.name: Paso Robles Willow Creek District
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Rolling hills (2014) west of Paso Robles town, with calcareous soils, cool marine air from the Templeton Gap and some of the region's most famous estates. Saxum's James Berry Vineyard, Linne Calodo and L'Aventure make dense, ripe Rhône and Cabernet blends here.

appellations.name: Templeton Gap District
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: The southwestern corner of Paso Robles (2014), where gaps in the Santa Lucia Range let ocean air and fog reach the vineyards. It is the coolest of the districts, with calcareous soils; Zinfandel has been grown here by Italian families since the early 20th century.

appellations.name: Paso Robles Highlands District
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah, Petite Sirah
appellations.summary: The high, remote southeastern district (2014), at 365 to 610 m, with the largest day-night temperature swings in Paso Robles, low rainfall and sandy alluvial soils. Large vineyards grow Cabernet, Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Paso Robles Estrella District
appellations.summary: Rolling plains (2014) northeast of Paso Robles along the Estrella River, warm and dry with alluvial terraces. Gary Eberle planted Syrah here in the 1970s, among California's first.

appellations.name: Paso Robles Geneseo District
appellations.summary: An area of low hills (2014) east of Paso Robles city, with old alluvial terraces, some calcareous soils and moderate warmth, rainfall slightly higher than further east. Bordeaux and Rhône varieties do well, and Cass and Tobin James are among its wineries.

appellations.name: El Pomar District
appellations.summary: A district (2014) southeast of Templeton on high, old alluvial terraces with calcareous patches, where some marine air from the Templeton Gap still reaches. Moderate temperatures suit Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; the name recalls the El Pomar ('the orchard') land grant.

appellations.name: Creston District
appellations.summary: A district (2014) in the southeast of Paso Robles around the hamlet of Creston, in foothills of the La Panza Range at 300 to 600 m. Mixed alluvial and granitic soils, low rainfall and a warm, dry climate grow Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Syrah.

appellations.name: San Miguel District
appellations.summary: The northern district (2014) around the town and mission of San Miguel Arcángel (1797), warm with alluvial soils along the Salinas and Estrella rivers. Large vineyards for Cabernet and Merlot.

appellations.name: San Juan Creek
appellations.summary: The eastern, hottest and driest of the Paso Robles districts (2014), in the upper Cholame and San Juan Creek valleys, with low rainfall and big vineyards.

appellations.name: Santa Margarita Ranch
appellations.summary: The southernmost Paso Robles district (2014), a single historic ranch near Santa Margarita that was part of the mission lands of San Luis Obispo. Cooler and wetter than most of Paso Robles; large vineyards of Cabernet and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Santa Maria Valley
appellations.summary:
A wide, funnel-shaped valley (1981, expanded 2010) that opens west to the Pacific, among the first AVAs in California. Morning fog, afternoon wind and a long, cool season (harvests can run into November) give Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with bright acidity and spice.

Bien Nacido Vineyard, planted by the Miller family from 1973 on benches above the Santa Maria River, has supplied scores of producers with vineyard-designated fruit; Au Bon Climat and Qupé share a winery on the property.

appellations.name: Santa Ynez Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary:
The broad valley AVA (1983) along the Santa Ynez River, running from Lompoc east toward Lake Cachuma, with a strong west-to-east warming gradient. It contains Sta. Rita Hills, Ballard Canyon, Los Olivos District and Happy Canyon, and is used for blends across them.

The valley is a textbook of how distance from the ocean controls style. At the western end, Sta. Rita Hills grows taut Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; in the middle, Ballard Canyon and Los Olivos ripen Syrah and Grenache; at the eastern end, Happy Canyon is much warmer on summer afternoons and grows Cabernet. The town of Los Olivos and Solvang, a Danish-themed village, are the tourist hubs, and the 2004 film Sideways was largely shot along this valley's roads.

appellations.name: Sta. Rita Hills
appellations.summary:
The cold western end of the Santa Ynez Valley (2001, expanded 2016), where the Santa Rosa Road and Highway 246 corridors run between hills of sand, clay and diatomaceous earth straight toward the Pacific. It is one of the coolest places in California to grow red grapes, and its Pinot Noirs combine dark fruit with high acidity, herbs and a saline edge; Chardonnay is equally tense.

Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict planted the Sanford & Benedict vineyard in 1971, proving the area could ripen Pinot Noir. The AVA was approved as 'Santa Rita Hills' and shortened to 'Sta. Rita Hills' in 2005 after Chile's Viña Santa Rita objected to the use of its name.
appellations.terroir: Marine sediments, sand, chert and diatomaceous earth; steady afternoon winds; many growing-season days under 25 degrees Celsius.
appellations.nerd_note: The 2016 expansion drew 41 objections arguing that the added land sat on a different landmass, a rare public fight over a few hundred acres.

appellations.name: Ballard Canyon
appellations.summary: A small, north-south canyon AVA (2013) between Buellton and Los Olivos, with about 7,800 acres. Its growers decided to focus on Syrah, which shows dark fruit and savoury, peppery depth on the canyon's calcareous and sandy soils. Grenache and Sauvignon Blanc also grow well.

appellations.name: Los Olivos District
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Grenache, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: An alluvial plain (2016) of about 22,800 acres around the town of Los Olivos, between Ballard Canyon and Happy Canyon, with 47 vineyards (about 1,120 acres) at approval. Moderate temperatures and well-drained soils suit Sauvignon Blanc, Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

appellations.name: Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot
appellations.summary: The eastern and warmest part of the Santa Ynez Valley (2009), a 23,900-acre canyon area with serpentine and rocky soils. Bordeaux varieties ripen here, and Star Lane, Grassini and Happy Canyon Vineyard make Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc. The name supposedly dates from Prohibition, when moonshine was made in the canyon.

appellations.name: Alisos Canyon
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2020) of about 5,800 acres in the hills between the Santa Maria and Santa Ynez valleys, near Los Alamos. A cool, foggy marine climate and sandy, calcareous soils suit Syrah and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Lodi
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Carignan, Petite Sirah, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Lodi (1986, expanded 2002) is a grower's appellation of about 540,000 acres and roughly 100,000 acres of vines in San Joaquin and Sacramento counties. It is California's Zinfandel capital, with hundreds of acres of vines more than 50 and some more than 100 years old, often own-rooted in sand. Cooling Delta breezes keep it fresher than the rest of the Central Valley.

The 'Lodi Native' project has bottled single-vineyard old-vine Zinfandels with minimal intervention to show site differences, and producers from Turley to Bedrock and Michael David buy Lodi old vines.
