Lodi's sandy soils matter for more than texture: phylloxera cannot move easily through sand, so many old vineyards were never grafted, and some own-rooted Zinfandel and Cinsault vines are more than 130 years old. Growers here developed the Lodi Rules sustainability standard in 2005, now used outside the region. The style ranges from big, ripe, oaky Zinfandel to lighter, fresher bottlings from young producers who pick earlier.

appellations.name: Mokelumne River
appellations.summary: The largest and most important Lodi sub-AVA (2006), on the deep, sandy alluvial fan of the Mokelumne River west of the foothills. It holds most of Lodi's oldest Zinfandel and Cinsault, own-rooted because phylloxera cannot thrive in such sand. Bechthold, Soucie and Royal Tee are famous old-vine sites.

appellations.name: Clements Hills
appellations.summary: Rolling hills (2006) in the eastern part of Lodi, with red, cobbly clay-loam soils on old river terraces; slightly warmer than the west. Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Iberian varieties.

appellations.name: Borden Ranch
appellations.summary: Hilly eastern Lodi AVA (2006) of cobbled, gravelly old river terraces at the foot of the Sierra, on the old Borden ranch. Bordeaux varieties and Zinfandel.

appellations.name: Alta Mesa
appellations.summary: A high, flat terrace (2006) in the northeastern part of Lodi, in Sacramento County, with shallow sandy loam over hardpan that limits vine vigour. It is warmer than western Lodi because it lies farther from the Delta breezes, and it grows Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Cosumnes River
appellations.summary: The northwestern Lodi sub-AVA (2006) on the Cosumnes River, close to the Delta and among the coolest, with heavy clay and alluvial soils; Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay and Zinfandel.

appellations.name: Jahant
appellations.summary: A small Lodi sub-AVA (2006) between the Mokelumne and Cosumnes rivers, close to the Delta, with clay-loam soils and cool afternoon winds. Zinfandel, Cabernet and Petite Sirah.

appellations.name: Sloughhouse
appellations.summary: The northeastern and warmest Lodi sub-AVA (2006), in Sacramento County in the Sierra foothills along the Cosumnes River, with red, cobbly soils. Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

appellations.name: Sierra Foothills
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Barbera, Syrah, Petite Sirah, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: A long umbrella AVA (1987) of about 2.6 million acres following the Sierra Nevada foothills through eight counties. Gold Rush vineyards of Zinfandel survive here, and the higher reaches grow Rhône varieties and Barbera.

appellations.name: California Shenandoah Valley
appellations.summary:
The core of Amador County wine (1983), a valley of rolling hills around Plymouth at 300 to 600 m, with decomposed granite and volcanic soils. It holds some of the oldest Zinfandel vines in California, including the Original Grandpère vineyard claimed to date from before 1869, and Deaver Vineyard, whose fruit made Sutter Home's 1968 Amador Zinfandel. Barbera and Rhône varieties also do well.

The name includes 'California' to separate it from the older Shenandoah Valley AVA of Virginia and West Virginia.

appellations.name: Fiddletown
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1983) in Amador County above the Shenandoah Valley, at about 450 to 760 m, with old Zinfandel vineyards such as Eschen, planted around 1910.

appellations.name: El Dorado
appellations.grapes: Zinfandel, Syrah, Barbera, Grenache, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: A high AVA (1983) in El Dorado County, near where gold was found at Coloma in 1848, with vineyards from about 365 to 1,070 m, among the highest in California. Volcanic and granitic soils and cool nights suit Rhône varieties, Barbera, Zinfandel and even Riesling.

appellations.name: Fair Play
appellations.summary: A high sub-AVA (2001, expanded 2015) around the hamlet of Fair Play in southern El Dorado County, at about 600 to 900 m on decomposed granite. Small family wineries make Rhône and Spanish varieties and Zinfandel.

appellations.name: North Yuba
appellations.summary: A small, high foothill AVA (1985) in Yuba County, created around Renaissance Vineyard, a winery founded by a spiritual community in the 1970s and known for long-aged Cabernet and late-harvest whites.

appellations.name: South Coast
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Viognier, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: Umbrella AVA (1985) of about 2.1 million acres covering the coastal portions of Orange, Riverside and San Diego counties, including Temecula Valley, Ramona Valley, San Pasqual Valley and San Luis Rey. Two further AVAs inside it were proposed by TTB: Rancho Guejito (2024) and Rancho Santa Fe (August 2026).

appellations.name: Temecula Valley
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Viognier, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Southern California's main wine district (1984), in Riverside County about 35 km from the Pacific. Cool air comes through the Rainbow Gap and Santa Margarita River gap each afternoon, and elevations of 300 to 450 m moderate the heat. Ely Callaway planted here in 1969; today there are dozens of wineries, mostly tourist-oriented, growing Rhône, Italian and Spanish varieties. Pierce's disease, spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter, devastated vineyards around 1999 to 2000.

appellations.name: Ramona Valley
appellations.summary: An upland AVA (2006) of about 89,000 acres in San Diego County, at 300 to 900 m around the town of Ramona. At approval it had 17 vineyards on about 45 acres; many small wineries now grow Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

appellations.name: San Pasqual Valley
appellations.summary: One of the earliest AVAs (1981), a small valley near Escondido in San Diego County. Its vineyards have mostly disappeared, but it remains on the TTB list. The proposed Rancho Guejito AVA would partly overlap it.

appellations.name: San Luis Rey
appellations.summary: A new AVA (2024) of about 97,700 acres in northern San Diego County around Fallbrook, Bonsall, Pala and Pauma Valley, named for the San Luis Rey River and Mission San Luis Rey de Francia (1798). At approval it had 44 vineyards on about 256 acres and 23 wineries. Marine air reaches the valleys through the river corridor.

appellations.name: Cucamonga Valley
appellations.summary: A historic AVA (1995) in San Bernardino and Riverside counties, east of Los Angeles. In 1900 Secondo Guasti founded the Italian Vineyard Company here and planted about 5,000 acres, then billed as the largest vineyard in the world; by the 1920s the valley had more than 20,000 acres of vines. Warehouses, freeways and Ontario airport have replaced most of them, but scattered old, dry-farmed Zinfandel and Mission vines survive, some more than a century old, and Galleano Winery (1927) still makes wine from them.

appellations.name: Malibu Coast
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: An AVA (2014) of about 44,590 acres in the Santa Monica Mountains of Los Angeles and Ventura counties, with about 52 small vineyards on 198 acres at approval. Ocean views and marine air, but also the constant threat of wildfire: the 2018 Woolsey Fire burned through many vineyards. Los Angeles County has since restricted new vineyard planting in the Santa Monica Mountains.

appellations.name: Saddle Rock-Malibu
appellations.summary: A tiny AVA (2006) of about 2,090 acres in the Santa Monica Mountains above Malibu, at 520 to 680 m, essentially the Semler family's Malibu Family Wines vineyard (planted 1997). Its hilltop vines produce Bordeaux and Rhône reds.

appellations.name: Malibu-Newton Canyon
appellations.summary: A bowl-shaped AVA (1996) of about 850 acres high in the Santa Monica Mountains, created around Rosenthal's vineyard, which was planted in 1987. Above the marine layer, it grows Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Palos Verdes Peninsula
appellations.summary: A small coastal AVA (2021) of about 15,900 acres on the hilly peninsula south of Los Angeles, with only about 7 acres of vines at approval. Uplifted marine terraces and constant ocean breezes.

appellations.name: Yucaipa Valley
appellations.summary: A new AVA (2024) of 36,467 acres in San Bernardino County, in the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains, with about 23 vineyards and two wineries at approval. Elevations of 600 to 1,500 m and cool canyon winds set it apart from the hot inland valleys.

appellations.name: Leona Valley
appellations.summary: A narrow valley (2008) in northern Los Angeles County that follows the San Andreas fault, at about 900 m, with cold winters and hot summers. About 20 acres of vines at approval.

appellations.name: Sierra Pelona Valley
appellations.summary: A small valley (2010) in northern Los Angeles County near Agua Dulce, at about 760 to 1,000 m, with about 96 acres of vines at approval. A high-desert-edge climate with big temperature swings.

appellations.name: Antelope Valley of the California High Desert
match: Antelope Valley of the California High Desert
appellations.summary: A large AVA (2011) in the western Mojave Desert in Los Angeles and Kern counties, at around 700 to 900 m. Hot days, cold nights, strong winds and very low rainfall; vineyards are small and irrigated.

appellations.name: Tehachapi Mountains
appellations.summary: A high mountain AVA (2020) of about 58,000 acres in Kern County, at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 m, between the San Joaquin Valley and the Mojave. Cool nights and big temperature swings; six small vineyards and one winery at approval.

appellations.name: Madera
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Tinta Cão, Orange Muscat, Black Muscat, French Colombard
appellations.summary: A warm Central Valley AVA (1985) in Madera and Fresno counties, known for fortified and sweet wines: Ficklin pioneered port-style wines from Portuguese varieties in 1946, and Andrew Quady's Essensia (orange Muscat) and Elysium (black Muscat) are dessert-wine classics.

appellations.name: Diablo Grande
match: refered by many newspaper articles as the  "Oak Flats Valley Ranch" or the "Oak Flats Valley"
appellations.summary: A single-development AVA (1998) in the Diablo Range foothills west of Patterson, Stanislaus County, created alongside a planned resort and golf community. It is cooler than the San Joaquin Valley floor below, but its vineyards are small and few wines use the name.

appellations.name: Salado Creek
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2004) of about 2,940 acres at the foot of the Diablo Range in western Stanislaus County, with 44 acres of vines at approval. Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga named Salado ('salty') Creek.

appellations.name: Tracy Hills
appellations.summary: An AVA (2006) of about 39,200 acres in the foothills southwest of Tracy, in San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties, with about 1,005 acres of vines at approval; afternoon winds from the Altamont Pass cool the area.

appellations.name: Paulsell Valley
appellations.summary: A foothill AVA (2022) of about 34,155 acres in eastern Stanislaus County, in rolling grazing land at the edge of the Sierra foothills east of Modesto. The petition stressed its rolling topography and soils, distinct from the flat, irrigated valley floor to the west.

appellations.name: River Junction
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2001) at the confluence of the Stanislaus and San Joaquin rivers in San Joaquin County, defined by river-borne alluvial soils and Delta breezes. It was created around a single large vineyard, and the name is rarely seen on labels.

appellations.name: Squaw Valley-Miramonte
appellations.summary: A foothill AVA (2015) of about 44,690 acres in eastern Fresno County, at 450 to 1,000 m on the western slope of the Sierra, much cooler than the San Joaquin Valley floor. Three wineries and a few vineyards at approval.

appellations.name: Willamette Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Gamay
appellations.summary:
Oregon's flagship AVA (1983, expanded 2016) of about 3.4 million acres, with most of the state's wineries and vineyards. Cool, wet winters and dry summers, with a long, mild ripening period in September and October, give Pinot Noir of red-fruit perfume, silk and bright acidity. Chardonnay has become a second calling card since the 2010s, made in a leaner, reductive style.

The valley's story is one of outsiders proving experts wrong. In the 1960s UC Davis advised that Oregon was too cold and wet for vinifera; David Lett, Dick Erath, David Adelsheim and Dick Ponzi planted anyway, choosing hillsides above the frost-prone floor. Today vintages swing between cool, rainy years that give translucent, high-acid Pinot and warm years (2014, 2015, 2018, 2022) that give richer, darker wines. Burgundian investment (Drouhin from 1987, Louis Jadot's Résonance, Lafon's Lingua Franca partnership, Roserock) and Champagne interest in sparkling wine have made the Willamette the New World's closest analogue to the Côte d'Or in spirit, though its soils (volcanic, marine sediment, loess) are quite different.

appellations.name: Dundee Hills
appellations.summary:
The birthplace of Oregon Pinot Noir and still its most famous address (2004). The Dundee Hills are a compact block of hills above the town of Dundee, and the AVA boundary follows the 200-foot contour, roughly where red volcanic Jory soil begins. Jory is deep, iron-rich, red clay loam weathered from Columbia River basalt that flowed here about 15 million years ago; it drains well and holds enough water for dry farming.

David and Diana Lett planted the first Pinot Noir in the Willamette Valley at their Eyrie Vineyards site in the Dundee Hills in 1965 to 1966, and Erath, Sokol Blosser, Domaine Drouhin Oregon (1988), Archery Summit, Domaine Serene and Lingua Franca followed. Dundee Hills Pinot Noir is classically red-fruited and perfumed, with silky tannin and a hint of earth and spice.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic Jory soils on southeast-facing slopes above 200 feet; protected from the worst Pacific winds by the Coast Range.
appellations.nerd_note: Jory soil is Oregon's official state soil, named after Jory Hill near Salem.

appellations.name: Eola-Amity Hills
appellations.summary: A north-south ridge (2006) northwest of Salem, directly in line with the Van Duzer Corridor, so cold ocean wind blows across it most summer afternoons. The wind keeps acidity high and skins thick; the soils are thin volcanic basalt with some marine sediment. Eola-Amity Pinot Noir is dark-fruited, firm and taut, and Chardonnay is among Oregon's best. Bethel Heights (1977) and Cristom were pioneers; Evening Land's Seven Springs Vineyard is famous.

appellations.name: Chehalem Mountains
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc
appellations.summary: The highest landform in the northern Willamette Valley (2006), a 30 km ridge southwest of Portland rising to about 500 m at Bald Peak. It has all three Willamette soil types: volcanic Jory, marine sediments and wind-blown Laurelwood loess. Adelsheim (1971) and Ponzi were early settlers; the AVA contains Ribbon Ridge and the Laurelwood District.

appellations.name: Ribbon Ridge
appellations.summary: A tiny ridge (2005) about 5.6 km long within the Chehalem Mountains, made of uplifted ocean sediments (Willakenzie soils) and sheltered by the larger mountains. At approval it had 14 vineyards on 286 acres. Beaux Frères (founded in 1986 by Mike Etzel with his brother-in-law Robert Parker) and Patricia Green made it famous for dark, dense Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Laurelwood District
appellations.summary: A sub-AVA (2020) of about 33,600 acres on the northern and eastern slopes of the Chehalem Mountains, defined by Laurelwood soil: wind-blown loess deposited after the Missoula Floods over basalt. At approval it had about 70 vineyards (975 acres) and 25 wineries. Laurelwood Pinot Noir tends to be lifted and spicy.

appellations.name: Yamhill-Carlton
appellations.summary: A horseshoe of low foothills (2004, boundary refined 2010) around the towns of Yamhill and Carlton, limited to elevations between 200 and 1,000 feet. Coarse-grained, ancient marine sediments (Willakenzie) drain quickly, and vines ripen early; the Pinot Noirs are dark-fruited and broad-shouldered. The AVA was approved as 'Yamhill-Carlton District' and later shortened.
appellations.nerd_note: Ken Wright's Carlton winery helped turn the town into a tasting-room hub; Shea Vineyard is one of Oregon's most bottled single vineyards.

appellations.name: McMinnville
appellations.summary: A sub-AVA (2005) in the Coast Range foothills west and southwest of McMinnville, limited to elevations of 200 to 1,000 feet, with uplifted marine sediments and basalt. Close to the Van Duzer Corridor, it is cool and windy, and the Pinot Noirs are dark and firmly structured. Eyrie's winery is in town, though its vineyards are in the Dundee Hills.

appellations.name: Van Duzer Corridor
appellations.summary: A low gap through the Coast Range (2018) about 59,900 acres in size, through which cold Pacific air flows into the Willamette Valley every summer afternoon, dropping temperatures fast. The AVA covers the valley floor and foothills where that wind hits hardest; at approval it had 17 vineyards on about 1,000 acres. Pinot Noir from here has thick skins, dark colour and high acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: The wind is so reliable that growers call it the 'Van Duzer winds'; TTB clarified Eola-Amity Hills' boundary when it created this AVA.

appellations.name: Tualatin Hills
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: The northwestern corner of the Willamette Valley (2020), about 144,000 acres in the hills west of Portland around Forest Grove, Gaston and Hillsboro. Laurelwood loess soils, higher rainfall and cooler temperatures than further south. At approval it had 33 vineyards and 21 wineries, including David Hill and Ernest Reuter's historic Forest Grove plantings.

appellations.name: Lower Long Tom
appellations.summary: The southernmost Willamette sub-AVA (2021), about 25,000 acres in the hills west of the Long Tom River near Monroe, between Eugene and Corvallis. Thin, uplifted marine sedimentary soils (Bellpine and Bellpine/Jory) and a slightly warmer climate. At approval it had 22 vineyards (492 acres) and 10 wineries.

appellations.name: Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2022) of about 5,850 acres around Mount Pisgah, a hill west of Salem near the town of Dallas. Its soils come from Siletz River volcanics, basalt about 40 to 60 million years old and much older than the Jory of the Dundee Hills. At approval it had 10 vineyards (531 acres) and two wineries, including Freedom Hill Vineyard, a famous source of Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Southern Oregon
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier
appellations.summary: Umbrella AVA (2004) joining the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, created so wines blended across them could carry a regional name. At approval it had about 120 vineyards, 3,000 acres and 17 wineries.

appellations.name: Umpqua Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Tempranillo, Syrah, Albariño, Riesling
appellations.summary: The 'hundred valleys of the Umpqua' (1984) around Roseburg, a tangle of small valleys where the Klamath Mountains, Cascades and Coast Range meet. It has the most varied geology in Oregon and a climate between the cool Willamette and the warm Rogue. Richard Sommer's HillCrest (1961) restarted Oregon wine here, and Abacela planted the Pacific Northwest's first Tempranillo in 1995.

appellations.name: Elkton Oregon
appellations.summary: The coolest and wettest part of the Umpqua (2013), about 74,900 acres along the Umpqua River near Elkton, only about 50 km from the Pacific, so marine air flows straight up the river. It is cool-climate Pinot Noir, Riesling and Gewürztraminer country, cooler than much of the Willamette.

appellations.name: Red Hill Douglas County, Oregon
appellations.summary: One of Oregon's smallest AVAs (2005), about 5,500 acres around a single hill near Yoncalla in the northern Umpqua, with red, Jory-type volcanic soil similar to the Dundee Hills. Essentially one large vineyard; Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Rogue Valley
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Viognier, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A large, warm valley system (1991) around Medford and Grants Pass along the Rogue River and its tributaries (Applegate, Illinois, Bear Creek). The eastern part around Ashland is high and continental; the west is wetter. Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet, Merlot and Viognier thrive; Peter Britt's Valley View (1852) at Jacksonville was Oregon's first recorded winery.

appellations.name: Applegate Valley
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Zinfandel, Viognier, Cabernet Sauvignon, Vermentino
appellations.summary: A sub-AVA (2000) of the Rogue Valley along the Applegate River, warm and dry with decomposed granite and alluvial soils. Small family wineries grow Syrah, Zinfandel, Viognier and Rhône and Bordeaux varieties; Troon converted to biodynamic farming.

appellations.name: Columbia Gorge
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Syrah, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: A dramatic AVA (2004) straddling the Columbia River where it cuts through the Cascade Range, on both the Oregon (Hood River, Wasco) and Washington (Klickitat, Skamania) sides. In about 65 km, rainfall falls from more than 90 cm a year in the west to under 25 cm in the east, so the gorge grows everything from cool-climate Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer near Hood River to Zinfandel, Syrah and Cabernet near The Dalles. Old Zinfandel planted by Italian immigrants survives at The Pines 1852 vineyard.

appellations.name: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo
appellations.summary:
The only AVA in the United States defined almost entirely by a single soil feature (2015). It sits on the Oregon side of the Walla Walla Valley, on the alluvial fan of the Walla Walla River, where the ground is a jumble of rounded basalt cobbles (Freewater cobbly loam) that store heat and radiate it at night. At approval it had about 250 acres of vines on 3,770 acres.

Christophe Baron, a Champenois, spotted the stones in 1996 and planted Cayuse; the Syrahs from The Rocks have a savoury, olive, smoked-meat and iron character often compared to the northern Rhône, sometimes called 'funk' by fans.
appellations.nerd_note: The AVA was the first in the US whose petition rested almost wholly on soil; it is entirely within Oregon, yet nearly all the wineries that use it are across the state line in Walla Walla, Washington.

appellations.name: Columbia Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary:
Washington's giant umbrella AVA (1984) of about 11.5 million acres covering most of eastern Washington and a strip of northern Oregon. Low rainfall, long sunny days, cold nights and Missoula flood soils give wines of ripe fruit and fresh acidity. Most Washington wine, including the biggest brands, carries this name. Inside it are 19 sub-AVAs.

The scale is hard to grasp: Columbia Valley covers about a quarter of Washington State, yet vines occupy only a small fraction, clustered on south-facing slopes and benches near the rivers where cold air drains away in winter. Growing degree days range from cool (Ancient Lakes) to very warm (Wahluke Slope, Red Mountain). Most vineyards are own-rooted on sandy, phylloxera-hostile soils, which lets growers replant quickly after freezes. The AVA also crosses into Oregon around Milton-Freewater and the Columbia Gorge, so some Oregon wineries use the name.

appellations.name: Yakima Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling
appellations.summary: Washington's first AVA (1983), along the Yakima River from Union Gap to near the Tri-Cities. It is the historical centre of Washington grape growing: Concord for juice, then wine grapes from the 1960s. Today about a third of the state's wine grapes grow here. The west end is cooler, the east end warmer; famous vineyards include Red Willow (planted 1973, an early source of Syrah) and Boushey.

appellations.name: Red Mountain
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary:
Washington's smallest AVA from 2001 until Candy Mountain arrived in 2020, about 4,000 acres on the southwest-facing slope of a low ridge near Benton City, at the east end of the Yakima Valley. It is one of the warmest spots in the state, with constant wind and very low rainfall; sandy, calcareous, rocky soils and wind stress produce small berries with thick skins.

The result is Washington's most tannic, concentrated Cabernet Sauvignon. Jim Holmes and John Williams planted Kiona and Ciel du Cheval in 1975; Hedges, Col Solare (Ste. Michelle and Antinori), Klipsun and Tapteil followed.

The sandy, calcareous soils over basalt are low in organic matter and very free-draining, so growers control vigour tightly with drip irrigation; vines are often own-rooted. Afternoon wind keeps the canopy dry and stresses the berries, shrinking them and thickening their skins, which is why the wines carry Washington's firmest tannins. The 2001 AVA was one of the first Washington appellations defined on such a small scale. Col Solare (founded by Antinori and Ste. Michelle), Duckhorn's Canvasback and Quilceda Creek's Galitzine Vineyard show how outside investment followed the reputation.
appellations.nerd_note: Despite the name, the mountain is not red; it is named for the cheatgrass (downy brome) that turns the slopes reddish in spring.

appellations.name: Rattlesnake Hills
appellations.summary: A sub-AVA (2006) of about 68,500 acres on the south-facing slopes of the Rattlesnake Hills north of the Yakima River, at 260 to 900 m, with many small wineries. Higher elevation and good air drainage reduce frost risk.

appellations.name: Snipes Mountain
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2009) of 4,145 acres on a single uplift rising from the floor of the Yakima Valley near Sunnyside. Its rocky soils include rounded cobbles carried by the ancestral Columbia River. William B. Bridgman planted vinifera on its slopes around 1917 and founded Upland Winery in 1934, and Harrison Hill Vineyard has Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1963, among the oldest in the state. Named for cattle baron Ben Snipes, who settled at its base in the 1850s.

appellations.name: Candy Mountain
appellations.summary: One of Washington's smallest AVAs (2020), about 815 acres on the southwest-facing slope of Candy Mountain near Richland, close to Red Mountain. Steep slopes, shallow loess and wind give dense Cabernet. TTB modified the Yakima Valley boundary to include it.

appellations.name: Goose Gap
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2021) of about 8,129 acres in the hills south of Red Mountain near Richland. At approval it had two vineyards covering more than 1,800 acres and one winery; the petition stressed geology and soils on the hill's folded basalt.

appellations.name: Horse Heaven Hills
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling
appellations.summary: A big AVA (2005) of about 570,000 acres on the south-facing slopes above the Columbia River, south of the Yakima Valley. Steady wind from the river reduces frost and disease. Champoux Vineyard (planted 1972 as Mercer Ranch) has given perfect-score Cabernets to Quilceda Creek and Andrew Will; Columbia Crest is based here. At approval there were 6,040 acres of vines.

appellations.name: Wahluke Slope
appellations.summary: A broad, south-facing alluvial fan (2006) of about 81,000 acres on the north bank of the Columbia, east of Mattawa, one of the warmest and driest places in Washington. Huge vineyards supply many wineries with ripe Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah.

appellations.name: Royal Slope
appellations.summary: A large AVA (2020) of 156,389 acres on the gentle, south-facing slopes of the Frenchman Hills, north of the Wahluke Slope. At approval 13 vineyards covered about 14,100 acres, many of them very large; the elevation and slope keep cold air draining away.

appellations.name: Beverly, Washington
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2024) of about 2,415 acres on terraces above the Columbia River at the hamlet of Beverly, just north of Sentinel Gap. It was proposed as 'Wanapum Village', but the petitioner asked for a new name after members of the Wanapum tribe objected to the use of their name, and TTB approved it as 'Beverly, Washington'.

appellations.name: Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: A cool northern AVA (2012) of about 162,800 acres near Quincy, named for lakes left in coulees carved by the Missoula Floods. Caliche-rich soils and a cooler climate make it Washington's best area for crisp Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris. At approval it had 1,399 acres in six vineyards.

appellations.name: White Bluffs
appellations.summary: An AVA (2021) of about 93,700 acres on a plateau east of the Columbia near Pasco, named for the pale cliffs of ancient lake sediments (the Ringold Formation) along the river. The plateau's flat top and south-facing slopes are cut by the Ringold and Koontz coulees.

appellations.name: Naches Heights
appellations.summary: A volcanic plateau (2011) of about 13,250 acres northwest of Yakima, at 365 to 640 m, formed by the Tieton andesite lava flow; its soils are wind-blown loess over that volcanic rock. At approval it had 105 acres of vines.

appellations.name: Lake Chelan
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Gris, Syrah, Malbec, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A glacial-lake AVA (2009) of about 24,000 acres around the southern end of Lake Chelan, about 80 km long and one of the deepest lakes in the United States. The lake moderates temperatures and extends the season. At approval it had 13 bonded wineries and 140 acres; Riesling, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Malbec now grow among apple orchards.

appellations.name: Rocky Reach
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2022) of about 32,000 acres on terraces along the Columbia River north of Wenatchee, near the Rocky Reach Dam. Its gravelly, rocky soils were deposited when the Missoula Floods and glacial outburst floods reshaped the canyon.

appellations.name: The Burn of Columbia Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (2021) of about 16,870 acres on a plateau above the Columbia River in eastern Klickitat County. The name is the one local residents have long used for the plateau; TTB declined to protect 'The Burn' on its own because the term is used elsewhere.

appellations.name: Columbia Hills
appellations.summary:
Washington's 22nd AVA (effective September 2026), about 29,387 acres in Klickitat County along the north bank of the Columbia River opposite The Dalles and around Maryhill. Eighty percent of the land lies within a mile of the river, which acts as a heat reservoir; soils are coarse basalt colluvium and wind-blown sand and gravel bars left by the ice-age floods, much coarser than the loess common elsewhere. At approval there were about 338 acres of vines owned by 19 landowners and four wineries.

The name comes from the Columbia Hills Natural Area Preserve and Columbia Hills Historical State Park, home to the petroglyph 'She Who Watches'.

appellations.name: Walla Walla Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Grenache
appellations.summary:
A celebrated AVA (1984, realigned 2001) shared by Washington and Oregon, around the town of Walla Walla at the foot of the Blue Mountains. Rainfall rises sharply toward the mountains (from about 300 mm in the west to more than 500 mm near the foothills), so some vineyards can be dry-farmed. Soils are wind-blown loess over Missoula flood deposits, plus basalt cobbles in The Rocks District.

Leonetti (1977), Woodward Canyon (1981) and L'Ecole No 41 (1983) built the valley's name for Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah; it now has well over 100 wineries. TTB proposed a Mill Creek-Walla Walla Valley sub-AVA of about 4,900 acres in August 2026.

Walla Walla is Washington's wine town par excellence: a small, historic farming town with over 100 wineries and tasting rooms in a valley that also grows its famous sweet onions. The valley shares its AVA with Oregon, and the Oregon side's cobbled Rocks District gives the Syrahs that made the area famous among sommeliers. A severe freeze in January 2024 damaged many vines, and growers continue to experiment with burying canes and frost protection.

appellations.name: Puget Sound
appellations.grapes: Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: A large AVA (1995) of about 4.5 million acres west of the Cascades, around Seattle and the islands of Puget Sound. Cool, cloudy and wet, it suits early-ripening grapes such as Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe, Müller-Thurgau and Pinot Noir. It is home to many wineries that buy grapes from eastern Washington, so the AVA name is used on only a small share of their wines.

appellations.name: Lewis-Clark Valley
appellations.summary: A low, deep river canyon (2016) of about 307,000 acres where the Snake and Clearwater rivers meet at Lewiston, Idaho and Clarkston, Washington, far lower and warmer than the Snake River Valley to the south. Before Prohibition it was a thriving wine region. At approval it had 16 vineyards (81 acres) and three wineries. TTB realigned the Columbia Valley to avoid overlap.

appellations.name: Snake River Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Malbec
appellations.summary: A huge AVA (2007) of about 5.2 million acres along the Snake River across southwestern Idaho and two Oregon counties. Vineyards mostly sit at 600 to 900 m on volcanic and old lake-bed soils (from Pliocene Lake Idaho), with hot days, cold nights and frequent winter freeze risk. At approval it had 15 wineries and 1,107 acres of vines.

appellations.name: Eagle Foothills
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: A sub-AVA (2015) of about 49,800 acres in the foothills north of Eagle, west of Boise, slightly higher and cooler than the surrounding Snake River Valley, with nine vineyards (67 acres) at approval. Bitner Vineyards and 3 Horse Ranch are known producers.

appellations.name: Finger Lakes
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Lemberger, Saperavi, Seyval Blanc, Vidal
appellations.summary:
One of the great Riesling regions outside Europe (AVA 1982), an area of more than 2 million acres around eleven long, narrow glacial lakes in upstate New York. The deepest lakes (Seneca reaches about 190 m, Cayuga about 130 m) store summer heat and release it in winter, protecting vines on the slopes from the worst cold and delaying spring budbreak until frost danger has passed. Soils are shale, limestone and glacial gravels.

Dr. Konstantin Frank proved at Keuka Lake in the late 1950s that vinifera could survive here, and his winery's first vintage came in 1962. Today Riesling is the signature, from bone-dry to ice wine, with tense acidity and slate-and-citrus flavours, followed by Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Lemberger, Gewürztraminer, Grüner Veltliner and Saperavi. The region has more than 100 wineries.
appellations.terroir: Glacial lakes moderate temperatures; slopes of shale, limestone and gravel; cold winters with snow cover.

appellations.name: Seneca Lake
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer, Lemberger
appellations.summary: The largest and deepest Finger Lake gives its name to a sub-AVA (2003) with more than 50 wineries on its slopes. The lake rarely freezes, so the 'banana belt' on its southeastern shore is the warmest part of the Finger Lakes, good for Riesling, Cabernet Franc and even Merlot. Hermann J. Wiemer, Red Newt, Ravines and Fox Run are here.

appellations.name: Cayuga Lake
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Cayuga White
appellations.summary: The first Finger Lakes sub-AVA (1988), on the slopes of the longest Finger Lake. Cayuga is deep enough to moderate the climate, though slightly cooler than Seneca; the Cayuga Wine Trail (1983) was the first organised wine trail in America. Riesling and sparkling wines lead.
appellations.nerd_note: Cayuga White, a hybrid bred at Cornell's Geneva station and released in 1972, is named for the lake.

appellations.name: Long Island
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: The AVA (2001) covering Nassau and Suffolk counties, surrounding the North Fork and Hamptons AVAs. Long Island's maritime climate gives a growing season of about 220 days, longer than upstate, and sandy glacial soils. Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and rosé are its strengths.

appellations.name: North Fork of Long Island
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The northern prong (1986) of eastern Long Island, between Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay, with most of the island's vineyards and about 40 wineries. Water on three sides moderates temperatures; well-drained sandy loam suits Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay in a fresh, Bordeaux-like style. Alex and Louisa Hargrave planted the first vineyard at Cutchogue in 1973.

appellations.name: The Hamptons, Long Island
appellations.summary: The southern prong (1985) of eastern Long Island, cooler and windier than the North Fork with heavier, loamy soils. Channing Daughters, Wölffer Estate and Duck Walk make Merlot, Chardonnay, sparkling wine and rosé for the summer crowd.

appellations.name: Hudson River Region
appellations.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Baco Noir, Riesling
appellations.summary: The oldest wine region in the United States still making wine (AVA 1982), along the Hudson valley north of New York City. French Huguenots planted vines in Ulster County in the 1670s, Croton Point had a commercial vineyard by 1827, and Brotherhood Winery has operated at Washingtonville since its first commercial vintage in 1839. The region pioneered hybrids after Prohibition; Benmarl, Millbrook and Whitecliff grow Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and Seyval Blanc.
appellations.nerd_note: Benmarl's vineyard at Marlboro is often cited as one of the oldest continuously planted vineyards in the US, dating to the 1770s.

appellations.name: Upper Hudson
appellations.grapes: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, Seyval Blanc
appellations.summary: An AVA (2018) north of the Hudson River Region around Saratoga and Albany, defined by its colder climate, which favours cold-hardy hybrids like Marquette, Frontenac and La Crescent; about 1,500 square miles.

appellations.name: Niagara Escarpment
appellations.summary: An AVA (2005) on the bench below the Niagara Escarpment in Niagara County, the US counterpart of Ontario's Niagara benchlands across the river. Lake Ontario's moderating effect and limestone-rich soils suit Riesling, Cabernet Franc and ice wine. At approval it had about 400 acres of vineyards.

appellations.name: Lake Erie
appellations.grapes: Concord, Niagara, Riesling, Vidal, Chardonnay, Catawba
appellations.summary: A three-state AVA (1983) along the south shore of Lake Erie in New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio, about 2.2 million acres. The lake keeps autumn mild, and the narrow strip between lake and escarpment is the largest Concord grape-growing area in the world, supplying Welch's juice; Welch's founder Charles Welch moved his operations to Westfield, New York in 1897. Wineries also grow Riesling, Vidal and hybrids. TTB proposed a Conneaut Creek sub-AVA in Ohio in 2024.

appellations.name: Champlain Valley of New York
appellations.summary: A cold AVA (2016) of about 500 square miles in Clinton and Essex counties on the western shore of Lake Champlain. TTB accepted that its short season suits cold-hardy hybrids (Frontenac, La Crescent, Marquette) rather than vinifera. At approval it had six wineries. A Champlain Valley of Vermont AVA across the lake was proposed in 2026.

appellations.name: Southeastern New England
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Vidal, Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A coastal AVA (1983) of about 2 million acres across Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the islands. The ocean extends the season by a few weeks compared with inland New England. Sakonnet Vineyards (now Carolyn's Sakonnet) in Little Compton, Rhode Island, petitioned for it; Westport Rivers in Massachusetts makes fine sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Martha's Vineyard
appellations.summary: An island AVA (1985) covering Martha's Vineyard, petitioned by Chicama Vineyards, which planted the island's first vinifera in 1971. Not to be confused with Heitz's famous Martha's Vineyard Cabernet in Napa. Little commercial production remains.

appellations.name: Western Connecticut Highlands
appellations.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: An upland AVA (1988) in western Connecticut's Litchfield Hills, with cold winters and a short season; Hopkins Vineyard and others grow hybrids and cool-climate vinifera.

appellations.name: Eastern Connecticut Highlands
appellations.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Cayuga White, Chardonnay, St. Croix
appellations.summary: An AVA (2019) of about 1,250 square miles in the hills of eastern Connecticut, with 16 vineyards (about 115 acres) and six wineries at approval.

appellations.name: Nashoba Valley
appellations.grapes: Albariño, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling, St. Croix
appellations.summary: A new AVA (effective April 2026) of about 18,367 acres in Worcester County, Massachusetts, around Bolton, Harvard and Stow, an old apple-orchard area west of Boston. The soils formed in glacial till and outwash; the most common series, Paxton, is a well-drained, deep loam. TTB accepted about 1,697 growing degree days (Celsius base), placing it in Winkler Region III. At approval it had three commercial vineyards on about 16 acres, growing Albariño, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling and St. Croix. Nashoba Valley Winery (1978), known for fruit wines, is the best-known producer.

appellations.name: Monticello
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Viognier, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Virginia's most important AVA (1984, expanded 2018), around Charlottesville in the Piedmont foothills of the Blue Ridge, named for Thomas Jefferson's home. Jefferson's vinifera failed, but modern growers on well-drained, clay-rich slopes make Virginia's best Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Viognier and Bordeaux blends. Barboursville, Early Mountain, King Family, Jefferson Vineyards and Michael Shaps are leading producers.

Charlottesville's wine scene grew from Gabriele Rausse's 1976 plantings at Barboursville and Horton Vineyards' bet on Viognier (from 1991), which led Virginia to adopt Viognier as its signature white. Petit Manseng, whose thick skins resist humidity, has become another local success. Summer rain and hurricanes remain the main threats, so growers favour well-drained slopes in the foothills (around 150 to 450 m), open canopies and early-ripening clones.
appellations.nerd_note: Jefferson Vineyards grows on land that Jefferson gave to Philip Mazzei for his 1774 vineyard experiment.

appellations.name: Middleburg Virginia
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier
appellations.summary: An AVA (2012) of about 190 square miles in Loudoun and Fauquier counties, horse country an hour from Washington, D.C. At approval it had 10 vineyards and 14 wineries. Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Chardonnay; Boxwood and RdV (founded by Rutger de Vink) make some of Virginia's most serious Bordeaux blends nearby.

appellations.name: Shenandoah Valley
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Vidal, Chambourcin
appellations.summary: A long limestone valley AVA (1982) between the Blue Ridge and the Allegheny Mountains in Virginia and West Virginia, drier than the Piedmont thanks to the rain shadow of the mountains. Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and hybrids; Bluestone and Barren Ridge are among its wineries. Not to be confused with California Shenandoah Valley.

appellations.name: Virginia's Eastern Shore
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary: A coastal AVA (1990) on the Delmarva Peninsula between Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic. Water on both sides moderates temperatures and extends the season; sandy soils. Chatham Vineyards on Church Creek is the leading winery.

appellations.name: Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace
appellations.summary: An AVA (1987) on the Northern Neck peninsula between the Potomac and Rappahannock rivers, where George Washington was born in 1732. Rivers and the Chesapeake moderate the climate; Ingleside Vineyards, which petitioned for the AVA, is the leading winery.

appellations.name: Virginia Peninsula
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot
appellations.summary: A coastal AVA (2021) of about 673,000 acres between the James and York rivers, including Williamsburg and Jamestown, where Acte 12 ordered colonists to plant vines in 1619. It was petitioned by The Williamsburg Winery; at approval it had five vineyards on about 112 acres.

appellations.name: Rocky Knob
appellations.summary: A small, high AVA (1983) on the Blue Ridge plateau in Floyd and Patrick counties along the Blue Ridge Parkway, near Rocky Knob. Cool, elevated and wind-swept; Villa Appalaccia makes Italian varieties here.

appellations.name: North Fork of Roanoke
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1983) in the valley of the North Fork of the Roanoke River in Montgomery and Roanoke counties, in the Ridge and Valley region of southwestern Virginia. Very few vineyards today.

appellations.name: Appalachian High Country
appellations.summary: A high, mountainous AVA (2016) of about 2,400 square miles straddling North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia around Boone, with vineyards from about 900 to 1,200 m, among the highest in the East. Short seasons and cold winters favour cold-hardy hybrids such as Marquette and Frontenac. At approval it had 21 vineyards (71 acres) and 10 wineries.

appellations.name: Outer Coastal Plain
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Albariño, Chambourcin
appellations.summary: New Jersey's largest AVA (2007, expanded 2017), about 2.25 million acres of sandy coastal plain in the southern half of the state. The Atlantic and Delaware Bay moderate the climate and give a long season; sandy, well-drained soils suit Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Albariño and Chambourcin. Renault Winery at Egg Harbor City has operated since 1864.

appellations.name: Cape May Peninsula
appellations.summary: A peninsula AVA (2018) at New Jersey's southern tip, surrounded by the Atlantic and Delaware Bay. The petition stressed its warmth: water keeps autumns mild and the frost-free season long. Sandy soils; at approval six vineyards on about 115 acres. Albariño, Merlot and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Warren Hills
appellations.summary: An AVA (1988) in the valleys of Warren County in northwestern New Jersey, where limestone valleys run between forested ridges of the Highlands. Cold winters favour hybrids such as Vidal and Chambourcin alongside cool-climate vinifera such as Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

appellations.name: Central Delaware Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1984) along both banks of the Delaware River in Pennsylvania (Bucks County) and New Jersey (Hunterdon and Mercer), sheltered by the valley; Unionville Vineyards and others make Chardonnay and Bordeaux varieties.

appellations.name: Lancaster Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1982) in Pennsylvania's Lancaster and Chester counties, in Pennsylvania Dutch farm country with deep, fertile limestone soils. Conestoga Vineyards petitioned for it; today wineries such as Waltz Vineyards grow Chardonnay and Bordeaux varieties alongside hybrids.

appellations.name: Lehigh Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Chambourcin
appellations.summary: An AVA (2008) of about a million acres in eastern Pennsylvania along the Lehigh River, named from a Lenape word for river forks. Rolling hills; at approval nine wineries and 220 acres. Galen Glen and Fox & Hound are known for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

appellations.name: Cumberland Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1985) in the limestone Cumberland Valley of south-central Pennsylvania and western Maryland, part of the Great Appalachian Valley that runs from New York to Alabama. The valley's sheltered floor and well-drained soils grow hybrids and vinifera for a handful of small wineries.

appellations.name: Catoctin
appellations.summary: A Piedmont AVA (1983) in Frederick and Washington counties, Maryland, at the foot of the Catoctin Mountains. Black Ankle and Sugarloaf Mountain are leading wineries nearby.

appellations.name: Linganore
appellations.summary: An AVA (1983) in Frederick and Carroll counties, Maryland, around Linganore Creek in the Piedmont. Linganore Winecellars (Berrywine Plantations), founded in 1976, petitioned for it and makes grape and fruit wines; the area grows hybrids and vinifera.

appellations.name: Yadkin Valley
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier, Chambourcin
appellations.summary: North Carolina's first AVA (2002), about 1.4 million acres in the Piedmont along the Yadkin River northwest of Winston-Salem. Former tobacco farmers replanted with vinifera and hybrids; more than 40 wineries make Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay and Viognier. Shelton Vineyards (1999) led the expansion.

appellations.name: Swan Creek
appellations.summary: A small sub-AVA (2008) of the Yadkin Valley in Wilkes, Yadkin and Iredell counties, with three wineries and 75 acres at approval; sandy-loam soils of the Brushy Mountains foothills.

appellations.name: Haw River Valley
appellations.summary: A Piedmont AVA (2009) of about 868 square miles along the Haw River in central North Carolina, named for the Sissipahaw people. At approval it had about 60 acres and six wineries.

appellations.name: Crest of the Blue Ridge Henderson County
match: Crest of the Blue Ridge Henderson County
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng, Riesling
appellations.summary: A mountain AVA (2019) of about 215 square miles in Henderson County near Hendersonville, defined by elevation (most land at 640 to 960 m) and a cooler climate. At approval it had 14 vineyards on about 70 acres and two bonded wineries.

appellations.name: Tryon Foothills
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot, Viognier, Chambourcin
appellations.summary: A new AVA (effective October 2025) of about 176 square miles in Polk County, North Carolina, around Tryon and Columbus, on the escarpment where the Blue Ridge drops to the Piedmont. Its key feature is a thermal belt: on calm nights, cold air sinks to the valley floors and warmer air settles on the mid-slopes, so frost is rarer there. The petition placed 95 percent of the area in Winkler Region V; at approval it had five vineyards (about 78 acres) and four wineries.

appellations.name: Upper Hiwassee Highlands
appellations.summary: A mountain AVA (2014) of about 690 square miles in the Hiwassee River basin straddling Georgia and North Carolina. At approval 26 vineyards grew about 54 acres of hybrids, natives and vinifera, and five wineries were operating.

appellations.name: Dahlonega Plateau
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Georgia's first wholly in-state AVA (2018), about 133 square miles on a plateau in Lumpkin and White counties, the site of the 1829 Georgia gold rush. Elevation and slope give better air drainage than the surrounding land. At approval it had seven wineries and about 110 acres; Wolf Mountain, Frogtown and Three Sisters grow Cabernet, Petit Manseng and sparkling-wine grapes.

appellations.name: Upper Cumberland
appellations.summary: A large AVA (2024) of about 2.19 million acres on the Highland Rim and Cumberland Plateau in Middle Tennessee, with 55 small vineyards (about 71 acres) and nine wineries at approval. The petition stressed limestone and sandstone geology, elevation, soils and climate.

appellations.name: Nine Lakes of East Tennessee
appellations.grapes: Chambourcin, Cabernet Franc, Muscadine, Vidal, Traminette
appellations.summary: A large AVA (effective April 2026) of about 4,064 square miles in the Valley and Ridge Province of East Tennessee, named for the nine reservoirs created by Tennessee Valley Authority dams in the 14 counties around Knoxville. Parallel ridges (about 330 to 460 m) and valleys let growers choose slopes where morning sun dries the dew. At approval it had about 232 acres of vines and 29 wineries, many of them busy tourist wineries around the Great Smoky Mountains gateway towns.

appellations.name: Mississippi Delta
appellations.summary: A large alluvial AVA (1984) of about 4.1 million acres covering the Mississippi Delta in Mississippi, Louisiana and Tennessee. The Rushing Winery petitioned for it; muscadines dominate the little wine made here.

appellations.name: Augusta
appellations.summary:
The first American Viticultural Area, approved on 20 June 1980, eight months before Napa Valley. It covers about 15,000 acres around the town of Augusta on the Missouri River west of St. Louis, founded by German settlers in the 1830s; before Prohibition it had a dozen wineries. Loess-capped bluffs and a valley moderated by the river grow Norton, Chambourcin, Vignoles and Chardonel. Mount Pleasant Estates (1859) is the anchor winery.

Augusta's 19th-century winemakers were mostly German immigrants, many of them liberal refugees of the failed revolutions of 1848. The Missouri River Valley was dubbed the 'Missouri Rhineland'. After Prohibition the industry vanished until Lucian Dressel bought Mount Pleasant in 1966 and replanted. Norton, a native grape that thrives in humid summers, makes deep, inky, high-acid reds that are the region's calling card.
appellations.nerd_note: Augusta won the race to be first partly because the 1978 rules were brand new and its petition was simple: a small, well-defined valley with a clear historical name.

appellations.name: Hermann
appellations.summary: An AVA (1983) of about 51,000 acres (80 square miles) along the Missouri River around the German-founded town of Hermann (1837). By the 1880s Stone Hill Winery was one of the largest in the country, winning medals at world fairs, and the town's Norton, known locally as Cynthiana, became famous; Missouri adopted Norton as its official state grape. Stone Hill and Hermannhof restored the 19th-century cellars after Prohibition.
appellations.nerd_note: Adam Puchta Winery (1855) claims to be the oldest continuously family-owned winery in the US.

appellations.name: Ozark Highlands
appellations.summary: A large AVA (1987) of about 1.85 million acres on the Ozark Plateau of south-central Missouri, around St. James, with chert and limestone soils. Italian immigrants at Rosati and St. James grew Concord and Catawba; St. James Winery is one of Missouri's largest.

appellations.name: Ozark Mountain
appellations.summary: By area the largest AVA in the United States: about 33 million acres (around 52,000 square miles) of the Ozark Plateau in Missouri, Arkansas and Oklahoma, approved in 1986. It contains the Hermann, Ozark Highlands, Altus and Arkansas Mountain AVAs and is used mostly as a catch-all for wines from the Ozarks.

appellations.name: Arkansas Mountain
appellations.summary: An AVA (1986) of about 2.9 million acres in the Arkansas River valley and the Boston Mountains of northwestern Arkansas, petitioned by Al Wiederkehr. Swiss and German immigrants planted here in the 1880s.

appellations.name: Altus
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1984) around the town of Altus in western Arkansas, settled by Swiss and German immigrants in the 1880s. Wiederkehr Wine Cellars (1880) and Post Winery (1880) are among the oldest in the South; Mount Bethel and Chateau aux Arc also operate here.

appellations.name: Ohio River Valley
appellations.grapes: Chambourcin, Vidal, Catawba, Traminette, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: A huge AVA (1983) of about 16 million acres along the Ohio River in Indiana, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia. This was the scene of America's first commercial wine boom: Swiss settlers at Vevay, Indiana planted vines in the early 1800s, and Nicholas Longworth's Catawba at Cincinnati made 'sparkling Catawba' famous in the 1840s and 1850s. Today it is a broad umbrella for scattered wineries.

appellations.name: Kanawha River Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1986) in the Kanawha River valley of West Virginia, around Charleston, within the Ohio River Valley AVA. A small number of wineries grow hybrids.

appellations.name: Indiana Uplands
appellations.summary: An AVA (2013) of about 4,600 square miles in the hills of southern Indiana, carved out of the Ohio River Valley AVA. At approval it had 19 vineyards (about 200 acres) and 17 wineries, including Oliver Winery, the state's largest, and Huber's Orchard. Limestone karst geology; Traminette, Chambourcin and Vidal.

appellations.name: Shawnee Hills
appellations.summary: An AVA (2006) in the unglaciated hills of southern Illinois, between the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. The region had about 1,250 acres of vineyards in 1890; today about a dozen wineries grow Chambourcin, Norton and Traminette.

appellations.name: Upper Mississippi River Valley
appellations.grapes: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, St. Croix, Edelweiss
appellations.summary: The second-largest AVA by area (2009), about 19 million acres along the Mississippi in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin, including the unglaciated 'Driftless Area'. Cold winters limit growers to hybrids bred at the University of Minnesota and by Elmer Swenson, such as Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent and Brianna.

appellations.name: Lake Wisconsin
appellations.grapes: Marquette, Maréchal Foch, St. Pepin, La Crescent
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1994) of about 32,000 acres in Columbia and Dane counties, Wisconsin, on the Wisconsin River near Prairie du Sac. Wollersheim Winery occupies the site where the Hungarian Agoston Haraszthy planted vines in the 1840s before he left for California; its hillside caves were dug in 1858.

appellations.name: Wisconsin Ledge
appellations.grapes: Marquette, La Crescent, St. Pepin, Frontenac
appellations.summary: An AVA (2012) of about 3,800 square miles (2.4 million acres) in northeastern Wisconsin along the Niagara Escarpment, including the Door Peninsula. Lake Michigan and Green Bay moderate the climate; cold-hardy hybrids dominate.

appellations.name: Alexandria Lakes
appellations.summary: A small AVA (2005) of about 9,000 acres among the glacial lakes near Alexandria, Minnesota, created around Carlos Creek Winery and among the most northerly AVAs in the US. Cold-hardy hybrids.

appellations.name: Loess Hills District
appellations.summary: An AVA (2016) of about 4.6 million acres (some 7,200 square miles) along the Missouri River in western Iowa and northwestern Missouri, defined by its extraordinarily deep wind-blown loess soils, which form steep bluffs. At approval it had 66 vineyards on 112 acres and 13 wineries.

appellations.name: Loramie Creek
appellations.summary: A tiny AVA (1982) in Shelby County, western Ohio, created for a single farm winery; no longer commercially active, but still on the TTB list.

appellations.name: Old Mission Peninsula
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer
appellations.summary: A narrow, 30 km peninsula (1987) jutting into Grand Traverse Bay north of Traverse City. Lake Michigan surrounds it on three sides, delaying spring and extending autumn; cherry orchards share the slopes with Riesling, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Edward O'Keefe planted vinifera at Chateau Grand Traverse in 1974, Michigan's first commercial vinifera vineyard.

appellations.name: Leelanau Peninsula
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Gewürztraminer
appellations.summary: A peninsula AVA (1982) between Lake Michigan and Grand Traverse Bay, home to dozens of wineries. Larry Mawby, who petitioned for the AVA, is known for sparkling wine; Riesling, Pinot Noir and Gewürztraminer are the main grapes.

appellations.name: Lake Michigan Shore
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Vidal, Concord
appellations.summary: An AVA (1983) in southwestern Michigan near Lake Michigan, where lake winds protect vines from cold. It is Michigan's most productive area, with St. Julian (1921) and Tabor Hill (1968) among its wineries.

appellations.name: Fennville
appellations.summary: One of the first AVAs (1981), a small area near Lake Michigan in Allegan County around Fenn Valley Vineyards, which petitioned for it. Sandy soils and lake moderation.

appellations.name: Tip of the Mitt
appellations.summary: A cold AVA (2016) of about 2,760 square miles (1.75 million acres) at the northern tip of Michigan's Lower Peninsula, between Lakes Michigan and Huron. Cold-hardy hybrids dominate; 41 vineyards (94 acres) and 8 wineries at approval.

appellations.name: Isle St. George
appellations.summary: An island AVA (1982) of about 700 acres covering North Bass Island in Lake Erie, close to the Canadian border. The lake keeps winters mild and autumns long, and vines have grown here since the 1850s. Meier's Wine Cellars, which petitioned for the AVA, farmed much of the island's land in Catawba, Riesling and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Grand River Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Vidal
appellations.summary: An AVA (1983) in northeast Ohio along the Grand River near Lake Erie, where lake moderation and gravelly soils allow vinifera. Debonné Vineyards and Ferrante are leading producers of Riesling and ice wine.

appellations.name: Texas High Plains
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier, Roussanne, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: The engine of Texas wine (1993), about 8.9 million acres on the Llano Estacado around Lubbock, at 900 to 1,200 m. It grows the large majority of Texas wine grapes. Hot days, cool nights, wind and low humidity keep disease down, though hail and spring freeze are serious risks; soils are sandy loam over caliche. Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Viognier and Roussanne lead.

appellations.name: Texas Hill Country
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Sangiovese, Viognier, Blanc du Bois, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: By area the largest AVA wholly within one state (1991), about 9.3 million acres (some 14,500 square miles) west of Austin and San Antonio, centred on Fredericksburg. It is the heart of Texas wine tourism, with more than 100 wineries, though only a small share of the state's vineyards; many wineries use High Plains grapes. Limestone and granite soils; hot, humid summers. Two new AVAs, Llano Uplift and Hickory Sands District, were proposed inside it in 2026.
contains: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country

appellations.name: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country
match: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1988) of about 66,000 acres (roughly 100 square miles) around the German-founded town of Fredericksburg (1846). Sandy, granite-derived soils and the town's tourist trade have made it the epicentre of Hill Country wine; Pedernales Cellars petitioned for it.

appellations.name: Bell Mountain
appellations.summary: Texas's first AVA (1986), a single granite-and-sand hill north of Fredericksburg owned by the Oberhelman family. It would be enclosed by the proposed Llano Uplift AVA.

appellations.name: Texas Davis Mountains
appellations.summary: A high, remote AVA (1998) in the Davis Mountains of West Texas, around Fort Davis, with vineyards at about 1,500 m on volcanic soils, among the highest in the state.

appellations.name: Escondido Valley
appellations.summary: A small AVA (1992) in Pecos County, West Texas, where large vineyards were planted on University of Texas land near Fort Stockton in the 1980s, at about 900 m. The desert setting means intense heat and irrigation; the vineyards have long supplied grapes to Texas wineries.

appellations.name: Texoma
appellations.grapes: Blanc du Bois, Black Spanish, Cabernet Sauvignon, Munson hybrids
appellations.summary: An AVA (2005) of about 3,350 square miles along the Red River on the Texas-Oklahoma border, around Lake Texoma and Denison, where T.V. Munson worked. Pierce's disease limits vinifera; Munson's hybrids and Blanc du Bois do better.

appellations.name: Mesilla Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1985) along the Rio Grande from Las Cruces, New Mexico into far West Texas near El Paso, where Spanish friars planted Mission vines in the 17th century. Hot desert summers; St. Clair and La Viña are among its wineries.

appellations.name: Middle Rio Grande Valley
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Mission, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: An AVA (1988) along the Rio Grande from Santa Fe's southern edge through Albuquerque to Socorro. Spanish friars planted Mission vines near Socorro around 1629, the first in what became the United States. Gruet, founded by a Champagne family from Bethon in 1984, makes traditional-method sparkling wine here.

appellations.name: Mimbres Valley
appellations.summary: An AVA (1985) in the Mimbres River valley of southwestern New Mexico around Deming. Large vineyards here, many owned by European investors in the 1980s, supply much of New Mexico's wine grapes.

appellations.name: Sonoita
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Tempranillo, Malvasia Bianca, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Arizona's first AVA (1984), a grassland basin southeast of Tucson at about 1,500 m. Dr. Gordon Dutt of the University of Arizona planted test vineyards in the 1970s and founded Sonoita Vineyards in 1983. Red, iron-rich soils and monsoon rains in July and August; Callaghan Vineyards and Dos Cabezas made it known.

appellations.name: Willcox
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Tempranillo, Malvasia Bianca, Viognier
appellations.summary: Arizona's main growing area (2016), about 526,000 acres in a high basin around a dry lake bed (Willcox Playa) at about 1,300 to 1,600 m. At approval it had 21 vineyards on about 454 acres and 18 wineries; it now grows the majority of Arizona's wine grapes, mostly Rhône and Spanish varieties.

appellations.name: Verde Valley
appellations.summary: A valley AVA (2021) of about 200 square miles along the Verde River in Yavapai County, near Cottonwood and Jerome, at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 m. Maynard James Keenan of Caduceus Cellars helped lead its rise. At approval it had 24 vineyards (about 125 acres) and 11 wineries.

appellations.name: Grand Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Colorado's main wine area (1991), along the Colorado River around Palisade and Grand Junction at about 1,400 m. Cold air drains down the river canyon at night and warm air off the Book Cliffs reduces frost, making it fruit country (Palisade peaches) as well as wine country. Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Merlot.

appellations.name: West Elks
appellations.summary: One of the highest AVAs in the US (2001), along the North Fork of the Gunnison River around Paonia and Hotchkiss, at about 1,700 to 1,900 m. Cool and high, it grows Pinot Noir, Riesling and Gewürztraminer; Stone Cottage and Azura are among its small wineries.

appellations.name: Ulupalakua
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Grenache, Chenin Blanc, Viognier
appellations.summary: The smallest AVA in the United States (2021), about 70 acres on the leeward slopes of Haleakalā on Maui, at around 600 m, with about 16 acres of vines at approval. It is essentially MauiWine's estate on the historic Ulupalakua Ranch, where Emil Tedeschi planted grapes in 1974; volcanic soils and trade winds suit Syrah, Malbec and Chenin Blanc, and MauiWine also makes pineapple wine.

appellations.name: Niagara Peninsula
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Gamay, Vidal
appellations.summary:
Canada's largest appellation and the source of most Ontario VQA wine: 13,600 acres and 105 wineries in 2024 to 2025. The Niagara Escarpment and Lake Ontario create a protected corridor where over 40 varieties ripen. Benchland vineyards along the escarpment give the most structured Riesling and Chardonnay; the warmer lake plain gives Cabernet Franc, Merlot and much of Ontario's icewine.

The Niagara Escarpment, a limestone ridge that runs from New York to Wisconsin and is a UNESCO biosphere reserve in Ontario, is the key to the appellation. Air off Lake Ontario hits the escarpment and circulates back, so the benches stay a few degrees warmer on cold winter nights and cooler in summer heat. Even so, deep freezes (as in the polar-vortex winters of 2014 and 2015) can kill buds, so growers bury graft unions, run wind machines and plant hardy varieties. Niagara's best Chardonnay and Riesling are among the finest cool-climate wines in North America.

appellations.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Riesling, Vidal
appellations.summary: A regional appellation covering the plain below the escarpment between St. Catharines and the Niagara River, with four sub-appellations. It is the warmest, most-visited part of Niagara (39 wineries, about 1,597 growing degree days) and the heartland of Ontario icewine and Bordeaux reds.

appellations.name: Niagara Escarpment
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Gamay
appellations.summary: A regional appellation joining the three bench sub-appellations (Short Hills, Twenty Mile, Beamsville) along the escarpment between St. Catharines and Grimsby, with 25 wineries. Fossil-rich limestone and dolomite soils, slopes and lake breezes give Ontario's most mineral Riesling and Chardonnay. Not to be confused with the US Niagara Escarpment AVA across the river in New York.

appellations.name: Niagara River
appellations.summary: Sub-appellation (Niagara-on-the-Lake) along the Niagara River, where the deep, fast-moving river carries warm air and keeps frost away; about 1,606 growing degree days and 199 frost-free days. Warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot as well as icewine.

appellations.name: Niagara Lakeshore
appellations.summary: Sub-appellation on the shore of Lake Ontario around the town of Niagara-on-the-Lake, with the longest frost-free season in Niagara (about 213 days) and around 1,563 growing degree days; lake breezes keep it frost-free late into autumn.

appellations.name: Four Mile Creek
appellations.summary: Sub-appellation on the flat plain of Niagara-on-the-Lake around Four Mile Creek, with heavy clay-loam soils and about 1,582 growing degree days; warm, early-ripening sites for Cabernet Franc, Merlot and icewine Vidal.

appellations.name: St. David's Bench
appellations.summary: A raised bench at the foot of the escarpment around St. Davids, with the highest heat accumulation in Niagara (about 1,637 growing degree days); well-drained, sloping soils over the escarpment's lower terrace. Château des Charmes's château stands here.

appellations.name: Short Hills Bench
appellations.summary: The easternmost escarpment bench, a hilly area southwest of St. Catharines around Twelve Mile Creek; relatively far from the lake, it has hot summers but fewer frost-free days (about 187). Henry of Pelham's family estate dates to a land grant of 1794.

appellations.name: Twenty Mile Bench
appellations.summary: A bench sub-appellation around Jordan and Vineland, cut by Twenty Mile Creek ravines, with steep, limestone-rich slopes and cooling breezes (about 1,523 growing degree days). Home of Cave Spring (1986) and Tawse and some of Ontario's best Riesling and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Beamsville Bench
appellations.summary: The western escarpment bench around Beamsville, with steep, northward-facing slopes, well-drained clay-loam over dolomitic limestone and the most frost-free days on the escarpment (about 217); 12 wineries. Known for taut Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

appellations.name: Creek Shores
appellations.summary: A lakeshore-plain sub-appellation between St. Catharines and Jordan, crossed by creeks (Twenty Mile, Fifteen Mile, Sixteen Mile) that drain the escarpment; about 1,550 growing degree days. Lake Ontario and the creeks moderate temperatures.

appellations.name: Lincoln Lakeshore
appellations.summary: A flat, lake-cooled sub-appellation along Lake Ontario in the Town of Lincoln, with a long frost-free season (about 198 days) but cooler summers (about 1,527 growing degree days); it supplies grapes to many Niagara wineries.

appellations.name: Vinemount Ridge
appellations.summary: The highest and coolest Niagara sub-appellation, on the top ridge of the escarpment above the benches, with the shortest frost-free season (about 178 days) and lowest heat (about 1,469 growing degree days). Riesling and icewine thrive; cold winters are a risk.

appellations.name: Lake Erie North Shore
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Riesling, Chardonnay, Vidal
appellations.summary: Ontario's southernmost and warmest mainland appellation, a bow-shaped strip along Lake Erie from Amherstburg to near St. Thomas at about 42 degrees north. Shallow Lake Erie warms quickly, giving more growing degree days than any other Ontario region; red Bordeaux varieties ripen well. Colio Estate (1980) at Harrow is the oldest modern winery; about 15 wineries.

appellations.name: South Islands
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Vidal
appellations.summary: A sub-appellation (July 2015) covering the nine islands of the Township of Pelee in Lake Erie, at Canada's southernmost point. Grapes grow mainly on Pelee Island, about 20 km offshore, where the growing season can be 30 days longer than on the mainland and harvest begins in August. Vin Villa, Canada's first commercial winery, opened here in 1866; Pelee Island Winery farms the island's vineyards on sandy loam and clay over limestone.

appellations.name: Prince Edward County
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary:
Ontario's newest and coolest primary appellation (2007), an island-like county in Lake Ontario east of Toronto. Shallow clay loam over fractured Trenton limestone drew winemakers looking for Burgundian conditions; the downside is winter cold so severe that many growers bury their vines under soil each autumn and dig them out in spring. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are taut, mineral and low in alcohol; Norman Hardie, Closson Chase, Hinterland (sparkling) and Rosehall Run are leading names.

Burying vines is labour-intensive: in late autumn, growers prune and lay canes in a trench and cover them with soil, then uncover them in spring. That helps them survive winter lows that can fall below minus 25 degrees Celsius. The County has a few dozen wineries, many of them small and family-run, and its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay have drawn comparisons to Burgundy's cooler villages.

appellations.name: Okanagan Valley
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling
appellations.summary:
BC's dominant GI, with about 90 percent of the province's vineyards along 175 km of glacial lakes. It runs from the semi-desert around Osoyoos and Oliver, the warmest place in Canada for grapes, to cooler Kelowna and Lake Country. Bordeaux varieties and Syrah dominate the south; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and sparkling the north. Eleven sub-GIs (2015 to 2022) mark out its benches and slopes.

The valley's north-south axis and its chain of lakes create a steep climate gradient: the desert floor around Osoyoos is among the hottest vineyard land in Canada, while Lake Country, about 175 km north, is much cooler and suited to Riesling and sparkling wine. Long summer days at 49 to 50 degrees north give extra ripening hours, and cold nights keep acidity. The frosts of 2022 and 2024 forced many growers to rethink varieties, with more cold-hardy clones and the replanting of almost all damaged blocks by 2026.

appellations.name: Golden Mile Bench
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer
appellations.summary: BC's first sub-GI (2015), a 21 km-long, east-facing glacial bench and alluvial fans on the west side of the valley south of Oliver. Gravelly, well-drained soils and morning sun give ripe yet fresh Bordeaux varieties, Syrah and aromatic whites. The name dates from the gold rush at Fairview in the 1890s.

appellations.name: Golden Mile Slopes
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: A sub-GI covering the steeper slopes and higher ground above the Golden Mile Bench west of Oliver, with shallower, rockier soils and later afternoon shade; Bordeaux varieties, Syrah and whites.

appellations.name: Okanagan Falls
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Syrah
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2018) around the town of Okanagan Falls between Skaha and Vaseux lakes, with a varied mix of benches, granitic slopes and glacial lake sediments. Blue Mountain's Pinot Noir and sparkling wines made its name.

appellations.name: Skaha Bench
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2019) on the east side of Skaha Lake south of Penticton: a steep, west-facing bench of glacial silt, sand and gravel that catches afternoon sun reflected off the lake. Painted Rock's Bordeaux blends and Syrahs are the benchmark.

appellations.name: Naramata Bench
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2019) along the east shore of Okanagan Lake north of Penticton, with about 40 wineries on west-facing glacial benches and silt bluffs above the lake. Lake reflection and evening warmth suit Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah and aromatic whites; it is one of BC's most visited wine roads.

appellations.name: Summerland Bench
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2022) on the bench above the town of Summerland, with about 60 ha of vineyards and gentle, sunny slopes of glacial silt; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

appellations.name: Summerland Lakefront
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 805 ha along the Okanagan Lake shoreline at Summerland, including Trout Creek, where the lake keeps temperatures mild; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling.

appellations.name: Summerland Valleys
