appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 1,350 ha in the side valleys west of Summerland, including Prairie Valley and Garnet Valley, higher and cooler than the lakeshore. Orchards share the land with vines; cooler nights suit Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

appellations.name: South Kelowna Slopes
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 800 ha on the slopes above the east side of Okanagan Lake south of Kelowna, home to historic vineyards such as CedarCreek and St. Hubertus; cool, lake-moderated Pinot Noir and Riesling.

appellations.name: East Kelowna Slopes
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 2,900 ha in the hills east of Kelowna, higher and cooler, home to Tantalus, whose old-vine Riesling comes from vines planted in 1978.

appellations.name: Lake Country
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: The northernmost Okanagan sub-GI (2022), about 2,500 ha around Winfield and Oyama between Kelowna and Vernon. Cool and lake-moderated; Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and sparkling. George and Trudy Heiss planted Gray Monk's vineyard in 1972 and pioneered German and Alsace varieties here.

appellations.name: Similkameen Valley
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Riesling, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A narrow, hot valley GI west of the Okanagan around Cawston and Keremeos, walled by rock cliffs that radiate heat, with strong winds that keep disease low. It is known as Canada's organic farming capital; Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Riesling.

appellations.name: Fraser Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Gris, Bacchus, Pinot Noir, Siegerrebe
appellations.summary: A coastal GI in the lower Fraser River valley east of Vancouver, with a wet, mild climate; mostly early-ripening whites and Pinot Noir, and many wineries using Okanagan grapes.

appellations.name: Vancouver Island
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A coastal GI covering the island's southeast, sheltered from Pacific storms by the island's mountains. Cool and sunny in summer; Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega and sparkling. Cowichan Valley is its sub-GI.

appellations.name: Cowichan Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Vancouver Island's sub-GI, a warm pocket north of Victoria (its name is said to mean 'warm land' in Hul'q'umi'num). Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and sparkling wine from small family wineries.

appellations.name: Gulf Islands
appellations.summary: A coastal GI covering the islands between Vancouver Island and the mainland (Salt Spring, Pender, Saturna), in the rain shadow of the Olympic and Vancouver Island mountains; small producers of Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

appellations.name: Lillooet
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Riesling
appellations.summary: A GI (2018) in the Fraser Canyon around Lillooet, a hot, dry rain-shadow pocket with long summer days; a handful of wineries such as Fort Berens grow Bordeaux varieties and Riesling.

appellations.name: Thompson Valley
appellations.summary: A GI (2018) around Kamloops on the Thompson River, semi-arid with cold winters, where growers favour hardier varieties and site selection on slopes above the frost-prone valley floor.

appellations.name: Shuswap
appellations.grapes: Siegerrebe, Ortega, Pinot Noir, Maréchal Foch
appellations.summary: A GI (2018) around Shuswap Lake and Salmon Arm, north of the Okanagan, cooler and wetter, with a short season. Growers favour early-ripening vinifera such as Siegerrebe and Ortega and cold-hardy hybrids; Larch Hills claims one of the highest-elevation vineyards in BC.

appellations.name: Kootenays
appellations.summary: A GI (2018) in the mountain valleys of southeastern BC, chiefly the Creston Valley, a warm pocket near the US border; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

appellations.name: Vin du Québec
appellations.grapes: Frontenac, Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix
appellations.summary: Quebec's protected geographical indication for wine (IGP), requiring 100 percent Quebec-grown grapes, independent certification and production standards; it covers still, sparkling, fortified and late-harvest wines from hybrids and vinifera. Most IGP wines come from Montérégie and the Eastern Townships around Dunham.

appellations.name: Vin de glace du Québec
appellations.summary: Quebec's IGP for icewine, from grapes (mostly Vidal) frozen naturally on the vine and pressed while frozen, so only concentrated, sugar-rich juice runs off. Quebec's severe winters make icewine a natural speciality, sold alongside the province's ice cider.

appellations.name: Cidre de glace du Québec
appellations.summary: Quebec's IGP for ice cider, made from apples or apple juice concentrated by natural winter cold. Christian Barthomeuf of Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise is credited with inventing it around 1989; Domaine Pinnacle and La Face Cachée de la Pomme made it famous. Not a grape wine, but a Quebec signature alongside icewine.
producers: La Face Cachée de la Pomme

appellations.name: Tidal Bay
appellations.grapes: L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Geisenheim 318, Ortega, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Nova Scotia's appellation-style designation, created by the province's wineries in 2011 with a first vintage in 2012. Tidal Bay is a crisp, aromatic, low-alcohol white blend that must be at least 51 percent L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal and Geisenheim 318 (with 16 other varieties allowed), made from 100 percent Nova Scotia grapes and approved by a blind-tasting panel. It is meant to taste of the sea air of the Bay of Fundy and to pair with local scallops and lobster.

appellations.name: Valle de Guadalupe
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Zinfandel, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary:
Mexico's most famous wine valley, about 20 km northeast of Ensenada along Highway 3, the Ruta del Vino. Dominicans founded the mission of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe del Norte here in 1834; Russian Molokan families farmed the valley from 1905 (their museum survives in Francisco Zarco); L.A. Cetto and Domecq industrialised it from the 1970s; and Monte Xanic (1987), Château Camou, Adobe Guadalupe, Casa de Piedra and dozens of boutique wineries turned it into a food-and-wine destination, from 6 wineries in 1999 to about 150 in 2023.

The climate is Mediterranean, with hot days moderated by Pacific air drawn through the canyon from El Sauzal, and the soils are sandy decomposed granite. Reds dominate: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Grenache and blends that combine ripe fruit with a saline, slightly bitter edge. Water is the valley's crisis: vineyards draw on an overexploited aquifer, and salinity is rising.

appellations.name: San Antonio de las Minas
appellations.summary: A small valley just south of Valle de Guadalupe, on the road to Ensenada, where Hugo D'Acosta founded Casa de Piedra in 1997 and the teaching winery La Escuelita. Slightly cooler and more exposed to marine air than Guadalupe.

appellations.name: Valle de Santo Tomás
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A valley about 45 km south of Ensenada, site of the Dominican mission of Santo Tomás de Aquino (1791) and the vineyards of Bodegas de Santo Tomás, Baja California's first commercial winery (1888). Cooler, windier and with heavier soils than Guadalupe.

appellations.name: Valle de San Vicente
appellations.summary: A broad valley about 90 km south of Ensenada around San Vicente, with a Dominican mission founded in 1780. Warm and dry, it supplies grapes to many Guadalupe wineries and grows Cabernet, Tempranillo and Grenache.

appellations.name: Valle de Ojos Negros
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A high inland valley east of Ensenada at about 700 m, cooler at night than the coastal valleys, with snow on the surrounding mountains in winter. Monte Xanic and others grow fresh Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here.

appellations.name: Valle de la Grulla
appellations.summary: A small valley on the road south of Ensenada around Ejido Uruapan and Santo Tomás, also called Valle de Uruapan, with old Grenache and Carignan vines and a cooler, coastal-influenced climate.

appellations.name: Valle de Tecate
appellations.summary: The northernmost Baja wine area, around the border town of Tecate, at about 500 m. Rancho La Puerta's vineyards and small wineries grow Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

appellations.name: Valle de Parras
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: A spring-fed valley in the Chihuahuan Desert of southern Coahuila, at about 1,500 m, named for its wild vines. Casa Madero's Hacienda de San Lorenzo (1597) is the oldest winery in the Americas, and several family wineries and brandy distilleries surround the colonial town of Parras de la Fuente. Hot days, cold nights and spring water give structured Cabernet and Shiraz and crisp Chardonnay.
producers: Vinícola San Juan de la Vaquería

appellations.name: Sierra de Arteaga
appellations.summary: A cooler, higher wine area (around 2,000 m) in the mountains east of Saltillo, near the town of Arteaga, with apple orchards and new boutique wineries.

appellations.name: Querétaro
match: Vinos de la Región Vitivinícola de Querétaro
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Macabeo, Xarel-lo, Parellada, Pinot Noir, Malbec, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine, granted by IMPI and launched in April 2025, covering the wine region of Querétaro state. Vineyards sit around Ezequiel Montes, Tequisquiapan, Colón and Cadereyta at about 1,800 to 2,100 m, among the highest in North America. Days are warm, nights cold and summer rain coincides with ripening, so grapes keep high acidity and moderate sugar: ideal for traditional-method sparkling wine, which is the region's speciality. Freixenet de México at Ezequiel Montes, with deep underground cellars, has made traditional-method sparkling wine here since the 1980s; La Redonda, Viñedos Azteca, De Cote and Puerta del Lobo make still wines.

appellations.name: Guanajuato
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Guanajuato's vineyards lie around Dolores Hidalgo and San Miguel de Allende at about 1,900 to 2,100 m. Father Miguel Hidalgo taught his parishioners at Dolores to grow vines before the 1810 War of Independence, and the viceroyalty had them destroyed; the area's modern wine revival began in the 2000s with Cuna de Tierra and now includes estates around San Miguel such as Dos Búhos and San Lucas.

appellations.name: Aguascalientes
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Merlot, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: A central state at about 1,900 m with a long grape tradition: brandy houses and a famous grape harvest fair (Feria de la Uva) in the 20th century, and 6,715 t of industrial grapes in 2025. Modern wineries include Vinícola Santa Elena and Hacienda de Letras.

appellations.name: Zacatecas
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Merlot, Ruby Cabernet
appellations.summary: A high-plateau state (about 2,000 m) that was Mexico's second-largest wine-grape producer in 2025 (26,024 t), mostly around Ojocaliente and Luis Moya, historically supplying brandy distillers. A handful of wineries now bottle Cabernet, Tempranillo and Merlot.

appellations.name: San Luis Potosí
appellations.summary: A high-desert state on the Altiplano with a small but growing number of wineries, part of the central highland expansion, at about 1,800 to 2,000 m. Like its neighbours, it relies on altitude for cool nights and battles summer rain and hail.

appellations.name: Chihuahua
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc
appellations.summary: Northern state with wineries around Delicias, Encinillas and Casas Grandes at high elevation, and mission vines at Cerocahui in the Copper Canyon, planted by Jesuits.

appellations.name: Sonora
appellations.grapes: Table and brandy grapes, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Mexico's largest grape-growing state, but mostly for export table grapes and for brandy, in irrigated desert around Hermosillo and Caborca. Wine production is small, though a few wineries have appeared, and the Jesuit missions of the Pimería Alta once grew vines here.

sites.name: Chateau Montelena
sites.text: Alfred L. Tubbs, a San Francisco rope maker, built this stone château under Mount St. Helena in 1882. Revived in 1972 by Jim Barrett, with Mike Grgich as winemaker, it made the 1973 Chardonnay that beat four white Burgundies at the 1976 Paris tasting and became the subject of the film Bottle Shock.

sites.name: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars (S.L.V. and FAY)
sites.text: Warren Winiarski bought land next to Nathan Fay's Cabernet vineyard in 1970 and planted S.L.V.; its 1973 Cabernet, from three-year-old vines, won the red flight in Paris in 1976. The estate bought FAY in 1986. Cask 23 is a blend of the two. Antinori has owned it outright since 2023.

sites.name: To Kalon Vineyard
sites.text: Hamilton W. Crabb planted these western Oakville benchlands from 1868 and called them To Kalon, 'the highest beauty'. Robert Mondavi built his 1966 winery on its edge. Today the vineyard is split among Mondavi (Constellation), Beckstoffer, Opus One and the Detert and MacDonald families, and its Cabernets fetch some of the highest grape prices in the country.

sites.name: Robert Mondavi Winery
sites.text: Cliff May's mission-style arch on Highway 29 marks the first major winery built in Napa after Prohibition (1966). Mondavi pushed cold fermentation, French oak, varietal labels and the dry, oaked 'Fumé Blanc', and he opened his doors to visitors when tasting rooms were rare.

sites.name: Opus One
sites.text: The joint venture of Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, announced in 1980 with the 1979 vintage. The half-buried limestone winery opened in 1991 opposite the Mondavi winery, and the wine is a single Bordeaux-style blend sold, in part, through the Bordeaux négociant system.

sites.name: Inglenook
sites.text: Gustave Niebaum founded Inglenook around 1880 and built the ivy-covered château in 1887. Under his great-nephew John Daniel Jr. it made Cabernets such as the 1941 that are still counted among the greatest American wines. Francis Ford Coppola bought it in 1975 and restored the Inglenook name in 2011.

sites.name: Beaulieu Vineyard
sites.text: Georges de Latour founded Beaulieu in 1900 and kept it alive through Prohibition with sacramental wine for the Catholic Church. From 1938 André Tchelistcheff introduced cold fermentation, malolactic control and small French oak here, and the Georges de Latour Private Reserve (first vintage 1936) set the template for Napa Cabernet.

sites.name: Schramsberg Vineyards
sites.text: Jacob Schram, a German barber, planted here in 1862 and dug caves with Chinese labourers; Robert Louis Stevenson visited in 1880 and wrote of wine as 'bottled poetry'. Jack and Jamie Davies revived the estate in 1965 for traditional-method sparkling wine, and their Blanc de Blancs was poured at Nixon's 'Toast to Peace' in Beijing in 1972.

sites.name: Harlan Estate
sites.text: Bill Harlan planted terraced hillside vineyards in the western Oakville hills from 1984; the first vintage was 1990. With tiny production and near-perfect scores, Harlan became one of the defining 'cult Cabernets' of the 1990s.

sites.name: Screaming Eagle
sites.text: Jean Phillips bought a small vineyard on the eastern side of Oakville in 1986 and released her first Cabernet, the 1992, by mailing list. It became the archetype of the cult Napa wine. Stan Kroenke and Charles Banks bought the estate in 2006.

sites.name: Dominus Estate (Napanook)
sites.text: Christian Moueix of Château Pétrus made his first Dominus in 1983 from the Napanook vineyard, once owned by Inglenook's John Daniel Jr. The 1997 winery by Herzog & de Meuron is built of basalt-filled steel gabions.

sites.name: Diamond Creek Vineyards
sites.text: Al Brounstein planted 8 ha on Diamond Mountain in 1968 and from 1972 bottled Volcanic Hill, Red Rock Terrace and Gravelly Meadow separately, the first block-by-block Cabernets in Napa. The Henriot family's Maisons & Domaines bought the estate in 2020.

sites.name: Martha's Vineyard (Heitz)
sites.text: Tom and Martha May's vineyard on the western edge of Oakville gave Joe Heitz a single-vineyard Cabernet from 1966, one of the first in California. Its mint and eucalyptus note made it famous; the 1974 is a legend.

sites.name: Heitz Cellar
sites.text: Joe and Alice Heitz founded their winery in 1961 and made Martha's Vineyard Cabernet one of the first famous single-vineyard wines in America. The Heitz 1970 Martha's Vineyard topped one of the 1986 Paris rematch tastings.

sites.name: Mayacamas Vineyards
sites.text: John Henry Fisher built the stone winery high on Mt. Veeder in 1889. Under Bob and Elinor Travers (1968 to 2013) it made slow-ageing Cabernet; the 1971 was in the 1976 Paris tasting and tied for third in the 2006 rematch.

sites.name: Charles Krug Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1861 by Prussian immigrant Charles Krug, Napa's first commercial winery. Cesare Mondavi bought it in 1943; a family quarrel there in 1965 sent his son Robert off to build his own winery at Oakville.

sites.name: Beringer Rhine House
sites.text: Jacob and Frederick Beringer founded the winery in 1876 and dug tunnels into the hillside; Frederick's 1884 Rhine House copies the family home in Mainz. Beringer stayed open through Prohibition with sacramental wine.

sites.name: Trefethen (Eshcol winery)
sites.appellation: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley
sites.text: The three-storey wooden Eshcol winery was built in 1886 for the Goodman brothers to a design by Hamden McIntyre. The Trefethens bought it in 1968; their 1976 Chardonnay was named best Chardonnay at the 1979 Gault-Millau tasting in Paris. The building leaned badly after the 2014 earthquake and was restored.

sites.name: Far Niente
sites.text: John Benson built Far Niente ('without a care') in 1885 with architect Hamden McIntyre. Abandoned after Prohibition, it was restored from 1979 by Gil Nickel and is known for Oakville Cabernet and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Domaine Carneros
sites.text: Champagne Taittinger's California sparkling house (1987), built as a copy of the 18th-century Château de la Marquetterie in Champagne and sitting on a knoll above Carneros vineyards.

sites.name: Buena Vista Winery
sites.text: Agoston Haraszthy bought this land in 1856 and from 1857 dug tunnels and built the first stone wine cellars in California. In 1861 he returned from Europe with more than 100,000 vine cuttings of over 350 varieties. The 1862 Press House still stands. Jean-Charles Boisset bought and restored the estate in 2011.

sites.name: Mission San Francisco Solano
sites.text: Founded on 4 July 1823, the last and northernmost of California's 21 Franciscan missions. Its vineyard of Mission grapes was the start of wine in Sonoma; after secularisation in the 1830s General Mariano Vallejo took over the vines.

sites.name: Gundlach Bundschu (Rhinefarm)
sites.text: Jacob Gundlach planted the Rhinefarm vineyard in 1858; Charles Bundschu joined later. The family survived the 1906 earthquake and Prohibition and still farms the land, making it one of California's oldest family-run wineries.

sites.name: Hanzell Vineyards
sites.text: James D. Zellerbach, a paper magnate and US ambassador to Italy, planted Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here in 1953 and built a small winery modelled on Clos de Vougeot. Hanzell is credited with introducing French oak barrels and temperature-controlled stainless steel to California winemaking. Its Pinot Noir vineyard is among the oldest in the state.

sites.name: Monte Rosso Vineyard
sites.text: A red-soiled vineyard high on the Mayacamas above the Sonoma Valley, planted in the 1880s by Emmanuel Goldstein and bought by Louis M. Martini in 1938. Its own-rooted Zinfandel and old Cabernet supply Martini and a string of small producers.

sites.name: Williams Selyem
sites.text: Burt Williams and Ed Selyem made their first Pinot Noir in 1981 in a garage, buying grapes from Rochioli and others along Westside Road. Their single-vineyard Pinots became the cult wines of the Russian River Valley; John Dyson bought the winery in 1998.

sites.name: Rochioli Vineyards
sites.text: The Rochioli family has farmed on Westside Road since the 1930s and planted Pinot Noir in the late 1960s. Its East Block, West Block and other parcels supplied the wines that built Williams Selyem's and Gary Farrell's reputations.

sites.name: Kistler Vineyards
sites.text: Steve Kistler and Mark Bixler made their first wines in 1979; from the Vine Hill Road winery in the Russian River Valley they produced dense, single-vineyard Chardonnays and Pinot Noirs that became benchmarks.

sites.name: Hirsch Vineyards
sites.text: David Hirsch planted vines on a remote ridge above the Pacific in 1980, astride the San Andreas fault. Fruit sold to Kistler, Littorai, Williams Selyem and others proved that the extreme coast could ripen Pinot Noir; the family now makes its own wines.

sites.name: Fort Ross
sites.text: The Russian-American Company's outpost on the Sonoma coast (1812 to 1841), where Russian settlers are said to have planted some of the first vines in northern California by 1817. Now a state historic park; the AVA above it borrows its name.

sites.name: Ridge Lytton Springs
sites.text: Ridge bought Lytton Springs in 1991, after making wine from its century-old Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Carignan since 1972. The straw-bale winery and its field-blend Lytton Springs bottling are a lesson in how old California mixed plantings work.

sites.name: Korbel Champagne Cellars
sites.text: The Czech Korbel brothers cleared redwoods here for lumber and turned to wine; from 1882 they made bottle-fermented sparkling wine. Korbel still uses the term 'California Champagne', allowed for brands grandfathered under the 2006 US-EU wine agreement.

sites.name: Simi Winery
sites.text: Giuseppe and Pietro Simi from Tuscany founded the winery in 1876 and built the stone cellar at Healdsburg in 1890. Isabelle Simi ran it for decades and kept it going through Prohibition.

sites.name: Iron Horse Vineyards
sites.appellation: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
sites.text: Barry and Audrey Sterling bought this foggy Green Valley ranch in 1976. Its traditional-method sparkling wines were served at the Reagan-Gorbachev summits and have been poured at White House state dinners ever since.

sites.name: Fountaingrove Round Barn site
sites.text: Site of the Fountaingrove community founded by Thomas Lake Harris in 1875, where Kanaye Nagasawa, a samurai-born Japanese immigrant, made some of California's most admired wines before Prohibition. The 1899 Round Barn survived for more than a century until the Tubbs Fire destroyed it in October 2017.

sites.name: Roederer Estate
sites.text: Champagne Louis Roederer chose the cool Anderson Valley in 1982 after a long search for a California site. Its estate-grown sparkling wines, especially the vintage L'Ermitage, are among the best traditional-method wines in the United States.

sites.name: Navarro Vineyards
sites.text: Ted Bennett and Deborah Cahn started Navarro in 1974 and made it the reference for dry Alsace-style Gewürztraminer and Riesling in California, sold mostly by mailing list.

sites.name: Ridge Monte Bello
sites.class: Monte Bello Cabernet: 1st at the 2006 Judgment of Paris rematch
sites.text: Osea Perrone planted on this limestone ridge in the 1880s. Four engineers from the Stanford Research Institute bought the property in 1959 and made their first commercial wine in 1962. Paul Draper's Monte Bello Cabernet placed fifth among the reds at Paris in 1976 and won the rematches of 2006, establishing it as one of the longest-lived wines of the New World.

sites.name: Mount Eden Vineyards
sites.text: Martin Ray, a purist who fought for honest varietal labelling, planted this mountaintop above Saratoga in the 1940s. The estate, run by Jeffrey Patterson since 1981, makes long-lived Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet from 'Mount Eden' clones descended from old California selections.

sites.name: Calera (Mt. Harlan)
sites.text: Josh Jensen found limestone and an old lime kiln (calera in Spanish) high in the Gabilan Range and planted Pinot Noir from 1975. Calera's single-parcel Pinots from Mt. Harlan are among California's most Burgundian.

sites.name: Calera Winery (Cienega Road)
sites.text: Calera's gravity-flow winery, built in 1977 into the hillside of an old limestone rock-crushing plant on Cienega Road, below its Mt. Harlan vineyards. The terraced building lets grapes and wine move by gravity from level to level, a Burgundian approach Josh Jensen chose before it was fashionable in California.

sites.name: Chalone Vineyard
sites.text: Vines were first planted on this limestone bench below the Pinnacles around 1919; some Chenin Blanc from that era survives. Dick Graff's Chalone made some of California's first Burgundian Chardonnays; the 1974 placed third among the whites at Paris in 1976.

sites.name: Pisoni Vineyards
sites.text: Gary Pisoni planted vines high on the family's cattle ranch in the Santa Lucia Highlands from 1982, using cuttings of disputed Burgundian origin. Pisoni and Garys' Vineyard Pinot Noir made the Highlands famous.

sites.name: Wente Vineyards
sites.text: Carl H. Wente bought land in Livermore in 1883. In 1912 Ernest Wente is said to have obtained Chardonnay cuttings from the vine nursery at the University of Montpellier; selections from them, the 'Wente clone', became the source of most California Chardonnay. Wente claims the first varietally labelled Chardonnay in America (1936).

sites.name: Concannon Vineyard
sites.text: Irish immigrant James Concannon founded the winery in 1883 and kept it alive through Prohibition with sacramental wine. In 1961 Concannon released the first varietally labelled Petite Sirah in the United States.

sites.name: Bien Nacido Vineyard
sites.text: The Miller family planted Bien Nacido ('well born') on old Spanish land-grant benches above the Santa Maria River from 1973. Its blocks are leased to and named by dozens of wineries; Au Bon Climat and Qupé built their shared winery on the property.

sites.name: Sanford & Benedict Vineyard
sites.text: Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict planted Pinot Noir and Chardonnay on Santa Rosa Road in 1971, the first vineyard in what became the Sta. Rita Hills. Its own-rooted 1971 blocks still produce, now owned by the Terlato family.

sites.name: Tablas Creek Vineyard
sites.text: Founded in 1989 by the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel and importer Robert Haas, who chose the limestone hills of west Paso Robles. Their imported Rhône clones, quarantined and propagated in their own nursery, went on to supply hundreds of American wineries.

sites.name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
sites.text: Founded in 1771, the third California mission. Its restored grist mill and mission-era water system recall the irrigated gardens and vineyards that supplied wine for mass.

sites.name: Old Palmtag-Almaden winery, Cienega Valley
sites.text: William Palmtag planted here in the 1850s. The old winery building sits right on the San Andreas fault, whose slow creep (about 1 cm a year) has visibly split the structure, a favourite stop for geologists.

sites.name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel (Trinity Vine)
sites.text: Founded in 1771, San Gabriel became the 'mother vineyard' of southern California, supplying Mission grape cuttings and wine. A vine in the mission garden, known as the Trinity vine, is traditionally said to be descended from the original planting and is often called the oldest living Mission vine in California.

sites.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
sites.text: Founded by Junípero Serra in July 1769, the first of California's 21 missions. Tradition credits it with the first planting of the Mission grape in what is now California; some historians favour San Juan Capistrano or San Gabriel for the first vintage.

sites.name: Guasti (Italian Vineyard Company)
sites.text: Secondo Guasti founded the Italian Vineyard Company here in 1900 and built a company town with a church and school. At its peak the vineyard covered about 5,000 acres and was promoted as the largest in the world. The old winery buildings survive next to Ontario airport.

sites.name: Galleano Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1927 by Domenico Galleano, a family winery that still farms and buys old, dry-farmed Zinfandel and Mission vines in the Cucamonga Valley, a living remnant of what was once the largest wine district in California.

sites.name: Bechthold Vineyard
sites.text: Joseph Spenker planted this Cinsault in 1886 on Lodi's sandy soils, and the own-rooted, head-trained vines are among the oldest Cinsault in the world. His descendants, the Bechthold family, still own it; Michael David farms it and it supplies producers from Turley to Bedrock.

sites.name: Sobon Estate (D'Agostini winery, 1856)
sites.text: Adam Uhlinger founded a winery here in 1856, later the D'Agostini Winery and one of the oldest in California. Sobon Estate now runs it, with a museum of Gold Rush-era winemaking in the old stone cellar.

sites.name: The Eyrie Vineyards (original vineyard)
sites.text: David and Diana Lett planted Oregon's first Willamette Valley Pinot Noir here in 1965 to 1966 against the advice of UC Davis. The 1975 South Block Reserve stunned French judges at the 1979 Gault-Millau tasting and in Drouhin's 1980 rematch. Eyrie also made the first Pinot Gris in the United States.

sites.name: The Eyrie Vineyards winery
sites.text: The Letts' winery in a converted turkey-processing plant in McMinnville, where Jason Lett now makes wine from his parents' old, own-rooted Dundee Hills vines. The family still releases older vintages from its library, showing how long Willamette Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris can age.

sites.name: Domaine Drouhin Oregon
sites.text: Robert Drouhin of Beaune, impressed by Eyrie's showing in 1979 and 1980, bought land in the Dundee Hills and opened this multi-level gravity-flow winery in 1988, the first major Burgundian investment in Oregon. Véronique Drouhin-Boss makes the wines.

sites.name: Sokol Blosser
sites.text: Bill Sokol Blosser and Susan Sokol Blosser planted in the Dundee Hills in 1971; in 2002 their winery was the first in the US to earn LEED certification for a green building.

sites.name: HillCrest Vineyard
sites.text: Richard Sommer, a UC Davis student, planted Riesling and other varieties near Roseburg in 1961 and founded what is regarded as Oregon's oldest continuously operating estate winery; he also planted the state's first post-Prohibition Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Abacela
sites.text: Earl and Hilda Jones searched the West for a climate like Spain's Ribera del Duero and planted Tempranillo here in 1995, Oregon's first. They also pioneered Albariño in the Pacific Northwest.

sites.name: Cayuse Vineyards (The Rocks)
sites.text: Christophe Baron noticed the cobblestone fields south of Walla Walla in 1996 and planted the Cailloux vineyard in 1997, farmed biodynamically. Cayuse's Syrahs and Grenaches (Bionic Frog, God Only Knows) became cult wines.

sites.name: Ciel du Cheval Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1975 by Jim Holmes and John Williams (who also founded Kiona), one of the first vineyards on Red Mountain. Its Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah supply a who's who of Washington wineries.

sites.name: Champoux Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1972 as part of Mercer Ranch and farmed by Paul Champoux from 1989. Quilceda Creek's Champoux Cabernets helped put Washington among the world's great Cabernet regions.

sites.name: Leonetti Cellar
sites.text: Gary Figgins founded Leonetti in 1977 on land his Italian grandfather farmed; its 1978 Cabernet appeared on the cover of a national wine magazine and made Walla Walla famous.

sites.name: Quilceda Creek
sites.text: Alex Golitzin, nephew of André Tchelistcheff, founded Quilceda Creek in Snohomish west of the Cascades in 1979 and trucked grapes from eastern Washington. Its 2002 Cabernet was the first Washington wine to receive 100 points from The Wine Advocate.

sites.name: Chateau Ste. Michelle
sites.text: Washington's largest and best-known winery, whose roots go back to Prohibition-era companies; the château at Woodinville near Seattle opened in 1976. Its Eroica Riesling partnership with Ernst Loosen (from 1999) helped make Washington a Riesling powerhouse.

sites.name: Red Willow Vineyard
sites.text: Mike Sauer planted Red Willow in 1973 on the western edge of the Yakima Valley and, working with David Lake MW of Columbia Winery, planted some of Washington's first Syrah in the mid-1980s. A small stone chapel on the hilltop is a landmark.

sites.name: Ste. Chapelle
sites.text: Founded in 1975 by the Symms family and named for the Gothic chapel in Paris that inspired its original building, Ste. Chapelle led the revival of Idaho wine and remains its largest producer.

sites.name: Dr. Konstantin Frank Winery
sites.text: On the west side of Keuka Lake, Dr. Konstantin Frank, a Ukrainian-born viticulturist who had grown vinifera in the Russian cold, planted Riesling and other European vines in the late 1950s and released his first vintage in 1962. His success showed that the eastern US could grow vinifera, and his estate is still family-owned.

sites.name: Hermann J. Wiemer Vineyard
sites.text: Hermann Wiemer, from a Mosel winemaking family, planted on the west side of Seneca Lake in 1973 and ran a grafting nursery that supplied vinifera vines across the East. His dry Rieslings set the Finger Lakes standard; Fred Merwarth and Oskar Bynke now run the estate.

sites.name: Brotherhood Winery
sites.text: Founded by Jean Jacques, a French Huguenot shoemaker, who made his first commercial vintage in 1839; it survived Prohibition by making sacramental wine and is commonly called the oldest continuously operating winery in the United States. Its underground cellars date from the 1880s and 1890s.

sites.name: Pleasant Valley Wine Company
sites.text: Founded in 1860 near Hammondsport as one of the first bonded wineries in the United States; its 'Great Western' sparkling wine won a medal at the 1867 Paris Exposition. The stone cellars are on the National Register of Historic Places.

sites.name: Castello di Borghese (former Hargrave Vineyard)
sites.text: Alex and Louisa Hargrave planted Long Island's first commercial vinifera vineyard here at Cutchogue in 1973, starting an industry on old potato fields. Marco and Ann Marie Borghese bought it in 1999.

sites.name: Benmarl Winery
sites.text: Hilltop vineyard above the Hudson at Marlboro, said to have been planted in the 1700s and later worked by Andrew Caywood, who bred grapes here in the 19th century; illustrator Mark Miller revived it in 1957 and it holds New York Farm Winery licence No. 1.

sites.name: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello
sites.text: Jefferson planted European vines in the gardens below his house from 1770 and for decades tried to grow wine grapes, without success; he was also America's most ardent buyer of Bordeaux and Burgundy. The restored vineyard on the south terrace grows varieties he planted.

sites.name: Barboursville Vineyards
sites.text: The Zonin family from Veneto founded Barboursville in 1976 on the estate of Governor James Barbour, whose 1814 mansion, designed by Jefferson, burned in 1884 and stands as a ruin. Gabriele Rausse planted vinifera here when experts said it was impossible; Octagon, its Bordeaux blend, is a Virginia classic.

sites.name: Jamestown (Acte 12, 1619)
sites.text: At the first General Assembly of the Virginia colony in 1619, legislators passed Acte 12, requiring every householder to plant and maintain ten grapevines. French vignerons were later recruited, but disease defeated the vinifera.

sites.name: The Mother Vine (Roanoke Island)
sites.text: A giant Scuppernong vine at Manteo on Roanoke Island, reputed to be about 400 years old and possibly planted by Croatan people or the Roanoke colonists of the 1580s; often called the oldest cultivated grapevine in the United States. It is privately owned.

sites.name: Renault Winery
sites.text: Louis Nicholas Renault, sent by Champagne houses to find an American site for sparkling wine, founded this winery at Egg Harbor City in 1864. It survived Prohibition by selling 'Renault Wine Tonic' in pharmacies and is one of the oldest continuously operating wineries in the US.

sites.name: Biltmore Estate Winery
sites.text: The Vanderbilt family's estate at Asheville opened a winery in the old dairy barn in 1985; it is often described as the most visited winery in the United States, though much of its fruit comes from California and Washington.

sites.name: Stone Hill Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1847 by German immigrant Michael Poeschel above Hermann; by the 1880s it was billed as the second-largest winery in the US, with wines winning at world fairs. During Prohibition its arched cellars were used to grow mushrooms; the Held family revived it in 1965.

sites.name: Mount Pleasant Estates
sites.text: Founded in 1859 by Friedrich Münch, a German pastor and writer, in Augusta, the town that became America's first AVA in 1980. Its 19th-century cellars survive.

sites.name: Hermann Jaeger's Neosho vineyards
sites.text: Swiss-born Hermann Jaeger settled near Neosho in 1865 and bred more than 100 grape varieties from native species. Working with George Husmann, he shipped about 17 boxcars of phylloxera-resistant cuttings to France, and in 1893 France made him a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur. He disappeared in 1895.

sites.name: T.V. Munson Memorial Vineyard
sites.text: At Denison, Thomas Volney Munson studied native Texas grapes and bred hundreds of varieties. His rootstock recommendations helped France replant after phylloxera, earning him the Mérite Agricole in 1888; Cognac is Denison's sister city. Grayson College maintains this vineyard of his varieties.

sites.name: Val Verde Winery
sites.text: Frank Qualia, an Italian immigrant, founded Val Verde at Del Rio in 1883; it is the oldest continuously operating winery in Texas and survived Prohibition selling table grapes.

sites.name: Llano Estacado Winery
sites.text: Founded near Lubbock in 1976 by Texas Tech professors and others, it led the modern Texas wine revival and is one of the state's largest wineries.

sites.name: Eden Park (Longworth's Garden of Eden vineyard)
sites.text: Nicholas Longworth's hillside vineyard, which he called the Garden of Eden, grew the Catawba for his sparkling wine, America's first famous wine in the 1840s and 1850s. The land became Cincinnati's Eden Park.

sites.name: Lonz Winery (Golden Eagle), Middle Bass Island
sites.text: Golden Eagle Winery on Middle Bass Island was billed as America's largest winery in the 1870s; the castle-like Lonz building of 1942 stands over its old cellars and is now a state park.

sites.name: Chateau Grand Traverse
sites.text: Edward O'Keefe planted Michigan's first commercial vinifera vineyard here on the Old Mission Peninsula in 1974, when most local growers relied on hybrids and cherries. Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on the lake-moderated slopes proved that northern Michigan could make fine wine, and the family still runs the estate.

sites.name: Wollersheim Winery (Haraszthy site)
sites.text: Agoston Haraszthy planted vines on this hillside above the Wisconsin River in the 1840s before he left for California; Peter Kehl dug the stone cellars in 1858. The Wollersheim family has run it since 1972.

sites.name: Senecú mission area (first vines in the US, c. 1629)
sites.text: Around 1629 Franciscan friars García de San Francisco and Antonio de Arteaga planted Mission grapes at the Piro pueblo mission of San Antonio de Senecú south of Socorro, to make sacramental wine: the first wine grapes in what became the United States. The exact site is lost.

sites.name: Gruet Winery
sites.text: The Gruet family, Champagne growers from Bethon, planted vineyards near Truth or Consequences in southern New Mexico in 1984 at about 1,300 m and makes traditional-method sparkling wine in Albuquerque. Gruet Brut and Blanc de Noirs became some of the best-value American sparklers.

sites.name: Sonoita Vineyards
sites.text: Dr. Gordon Dutt, a University of Arizona soil scientist, ran test plots that led to Arizona's first AVA (1984) and founded this winery at Elgin in 1983.

sites.name: MauiWine (Ulupalakua Ranch)
sites.text: Emil Tedeschi and rancher Pardee Erdman founded Tedeschi Vineyards on the slopes of Haleakalā in 1974; the tasting room is the 19th-century King's Cottage, built for King Kalākaua's visits, a short drive below the estate vineyards that make up America's smallest AVA.

sites.name: Palisade wine country
sites.text: Orchards and vineyards on the Colorado River below the Book Cliffs, where warm air and canyon breezes protect fruit from frost. Most of Colorado's wine grapes grow within a few kilometres of this town.

sites.name: Inniskillin
sites.text: Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser received Ontario's first new winery licence since 1929 in 1975 and moved to the Brae Burn Estate in 1978. Their 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo 1991, putting Canadian icewine on the world map.

sites.name: Château des Charmes
sites.text: Paul Bosc, an Algerian-born Frenchman, planted Niagara's first large all-vinifera vineyard in 1978 when experts said it could not survive. The family's French-style château stands on St. David's Bench.

sites.name: Cave Spring Cellars
sites.text: Len Pennachetti and Angelo Pavan founded Cave Spring in 1986 in an 1870s apple warehouse in the village of Jordan; their Riesling and Chardonnay from Beamsville Bench and Twenty Mile Bench vineyards helped define bench terroir.

sites.name: Tawse Winery
sites.text: Moray Tawse's gravity-flow, organic and biodynamic winery near Vineland; it was named Canadian Winery of the Year several times and is known for Burgundian Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Pelee Island Winery
sites.text: Pelee Island Winery farms Canada's southernmost vineyards on Pelee Island, with its main winery at Kingsville on the mainland; it made Ontario's first successful icewine in 1983 (50 bottles).

sites.name: Vin Villa ruins, Pelee Island
sites.text: Kentucky planters Thaddeus Smith and Edward and William McCormick founded Vin Villa in 1866, Canada's first commercial winery, on Lake Erie's Pelee Island. Only stone ruins remain.

sites.name: Johann Schiller's Credit River vineyard (Cooksville)
sites.text: Around 1811, Johann Schiller, a German-born former corporal, made wine here from wild and cultivated vines; he is remembered as the father of Canadian wine. The site later became Clair House Vineyards. Today it is suburban Mississauga.

sites.name: Norman Hardie Winery
sites.text: Sommelier-turned-winemaker Norman Hardie planted on Prince Edward County's shallow clay over limestone in 2003 and showed that the County could make taut, low-alcohol, Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. His vines, like most in the County, are buried under soil every winter.

sites.name: Closson Chase
sites.text: A purple barn turned winery, founded in 1998 by a group including film-maker Deborah Paskus, among the first to plant Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in the County.

sites.name: Father Pandosy Mission
sites.text: Oblate missionary Charles Pandosy founded this mission in 1859 and planted the Okanagan's first vines for sacramental wine. Several original log buildings survive as a heritage site in Kelowna.

sites.name: Mission Hill Family Estate
sites.text: Anthony von Mandl's hilltop winery above West Kelowna, rebuilt in 2002 with a 12-storey bell tower; its 1992 Chardonnay won a major award at the International Wine & Spirit Competition in London in 1994, a turning point for BC wine.

sites.name: Quails' Gate
sites.text: The Stewart family, among the Okanagan's pioneer farmers, planted grapes on the west shore of Okanagan Lake in the 1950s and 1960s and founded the winery in 1989; known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Chasselas.

sites.name: Nk'Mip Cellars
sites.text: Opened in 2002 by the Osoyoos Indian Band in partnership with Vincor, Nk'Mip (pronounced 'in-ka-meep') is widely described as the first Indigenous-owned and operated winery in North America, in the desert near Osoyoos.

sites.name: Burrowing Owl Estate (Black Sage Bench)
sites.text: Jim Wyse founded Burrowing Owl on the hot, sandy Black Sage Bench south of Oliver in 1997; its Merlots and Bordeaux blends helped define the south Okanagan style. Part of its proceeds supported the recovery of the endangered burrowing owl.

sites.name: Painted Rock Estate
sites.text: John Skinner planted a former apricot orchard on Skaha Bench in 2004; his Red Icon and Syrah were key evidence for the Skaha Bench sub-GI.

sites.name: Blue Mountain Vineyard and Cellars
sites.text: The Mavety family, growers since 1971, founded this winery in 1991; its traditional-method sparkling wines and Pinot Noir from estate vines anchor the Okanagan Falls sub-GI.

sites.name: Vignoble de l'Orpailleur
sites.text: Founded at Dunham in 1982 by Hervé Durand, Charles-Henri de Coussergues and partners, one of Quebec's first commercial wineries; it showed that Seyval Blanc and hilled-up vines could survive Quebec winters, and houses a wine museum.

sites.name: Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise
sites.text: Planted in 1980 by Christian Barthomeuf on slate slopes at Dunham, often cited as the first commercial vineyard of modern Quebec. Barthomeuf later invented ice cider.

sites.name: Domaine Pinnacle
sites.text: An orchard estate at Frelighsburg on the slopes of Pinnacle Mountain near the Vermont border, founded in 2000; its ice cider brought the Quebec invention to international markets.

sites.name: Benjamin Bridge
sites.text: Gerry McConnell and Dara Gordon planted vines in the Gaspereau Valley in 2002 with consultant Peter J. Gamble and Champagne-trained advisers; its long-aged traditional-method sparkling wines and Nova 7 put Nova Scotia on the world map.

sites.name: Domaine de Grand Pré
sites.text: Roger Dial opened Nova Scotia's first modern commercial winery here in 1979, beside the UNESCO-listed Acadian dykelands of Grand-Pré, reclaimed from the Bay of Fundy tides in the 1680s. Hanspeter Stutz bought it in 1993; it grows L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval and New York Muscat.

sites.name: L'Acadie Vineyards
sites.text: Bruce Ewert, who had made wine in British Columbia, founded this certified-organic winery in the Gaspereau Valley in 2004. It focuses on long-aged traditional-method sparkling wine from L'Acadie Blanc and on dried-grape (appassimento-style) reds that concentrate flavour in a cool climate.

sites.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
sites.text: The Norse site at the northern tip of Newfoundland (about 1000 AD), the only confirmed Viking settlement in the Americas. Sagas called the land the Norse reached Vinland for its wild grapes; butternuts found here show the Norse travelled south to where grapes grew.

sites.name: Casa Madero (Hacienda de San Lorenzo)
sites.text: Founded in 1597 when Lorenzo García received a land grant in the Parras valley, the Hacienda de San Lorenzo is the oldest winery in the Americas still in operation. The Madero family bought it in the 1870s; Francisco I. Madero, leader of the 1910 Revolution, was born in nearby Parras. Its Casa Grande Cabernet and Shiraz are among Mexico's best-known wines.

sites.name: L.A. Cetto
sites.text: Angelo Cetto, from Trentino, began making wine in Tijuana in 1928; his son Luis Agustín founded L.A. Cetto in Valle de Guadalupe in the 1970s, and it became Mexico's largest wine producer, known for Nebbiolo and Petite Sirah.

sites.name: Monte Xanic
sites.text: Founded in 1987 by Hans Backhoff and partners as the first premium boutique winery of modern Mexico; its Gran Ricardo Bordeaux blend became a benchmark.

sites.name: Casa de Piedra
sites.text: Hugo D'Acosta's stone winery (1997), whose Vino de Piedra helped show that Baja could make serious red wine. D'Acosta's teaching winery, La Escuelita, launched dozens of small producers.

sites.name: Museo de la Vid y el Vino
sites.text: Baja California's state wine museum on the Ruta del Vino, in a modern building set among vineyards at the entrance to Valle de Guadalupe. Its exhibits trace vines from the Jesuit and Dominican missions through the Molokan settlers and the Cetto and Domecq era to the boutique wineries of today.

sites.name: Museo Comunitario del Valle de Guadalupe (Molokan museum)
sites.text: In the village of Francisco Zarco, a small museum in an old Russian Molokan house recalls the pacifist Christian families who settled the valley from 1905 and planted its first commercial vineyards and wheat fields.

sites.name: Bodegas de Santo Tomás
sites.text: Founded in Ensenada in 1888 by Francisco Andonaegui and Miguel Ormart on former mission lands of Santo Tomás de Aquino (1791), Baja California's first commercial winery. It now farms the Santo Tomás valley.

sites.name: Freixenet de México (Finca Sala Vivé)
sites.text: The Catalan cava house Freixenet chose Ezequiel Montes in the 1970s; its traditional-method sparkling wines age in deep underground cellars, and it anchors Querétaro's wine route.

sites.name: Viñedos La Redonda
sites.text: One of Querétaro's pioneering wineries, founded in the 1970s on the high plateau near Ezequiel Montes at about 1,900 m. Its still and sparkling wines and busy harvest festivals helped turn the Querétaro wine and cheese route into central Mexico's main wine-tourism destination.

sites.name: Cuna de Tierra
sites.text: A winery near Dolores Hidalgo whose vineyards helped revive wine in Hidalgo's town; its name ('cradle of earth') nods to Dolores as the cradle of Mexican independence.

sites.name: Parroquia de Dolores (Miguel Hidalgo)
sites.text: From this parish church Father Miguel Hidalgo issued the Grito de Dolores on 16 September 1810. As priest he had taught villagers to cultivate vines, mulberries for silk and pottery, industries the Spanish crown restricted; officials ordered his vines destroyed.

sites.name: Cerocahui mission
sites.text: A Jesuit mission founded in the late 17th century deep in the Copper Canyon where mission-era vines are still tended and a little wine is made, a reminder of the colonial vineyards that once dotted the Sierra Madre.
